nodes.summary: The preface explains the purpose, difficulty grading, and solution-access arrangements for the book’s exercises, recommends independent work, and notes the value of practical algorithm experimentation alongside conceptual study. It announces a companion practical volume with Matlab software. The remainder is an acknowledgment of technical, institutional, editorial, permissions, figure, proofreading, and personal support received from named individuals and organizations, concluding with Bishop’s signature from Cambridge in February 2006.

structure.summary: The preface situates pattern recognition and machine learning as converging fields, emphasizing major recent advances in Bayesian and graphical modeling, approximate inference, and kernel methods. It introduces the book’s broad scope, intended audience, prerequisites, self-contained probability material, reference policy, and online supplementary resources. It also explains the role and use of the exercises, points to a companion Matlab volume, and acknowledges the many people, institutions, rights holders, and production contributors involved in creating the book, concluding with the author’s Cambridge signature dated February 2006.

structure.title: Mathematical notation
structure.summary: The text first establishes the book's mathematical scope and notation, covering vectors, matrices, intervals, identity matrices, functionals, asymptotic notation, expectations, variances, covariances, and data-matrix conventions. It then presents the complete contents of a pattern-recognition and machine-learning textbook, spanning introductory probability, decision and information theory; probability distributions; regression and classification; neural networks; kernels and sparse machines; graphical models; mixture models and EM; approximate inference; sampling; latent-variable methods; sequential data; and model combination. Each chapter's principal subtopics and exercises are listed, followed by appendices on data sets, probability distributions, and matrix properties.

nodes.title: 1 Introduction
1.1. Example: Polynomial Curve Fitting
nodes.summary: The text introduces foundational pattern-recognition tools and develops polynomial curve fitting as a regression example. Noisy observations are generated from sin(2πx), and polynomial parameters are fitted by least squares. It explains model order, closed-form optimization, underfitting, overfitting, generalization, RMS training and test errors, the effects of coefficient growth and training-set size, and the need for model selection. Regularization is then presented as a penalty on coefficient magnitudes, including its interpretations as shrinkage, ridge regression, and neural-network weight decay; it controls effective complexity but can also cause underfitting, with validation sets suggested for choosing complexity. The text concludes by introducing probability theory as a framework for uncertainty and optimal prediction, beginning with a two-box fruit example that defines random variables and long-run probabilities.

nodes.title: 1.2. Probability Theory
1.2.1 Probability densities
nodes.summary: The text explains Bayes’ theorem through a fruit-box example, distinguishing prior and posterior probabilities and showing how evidence can overturn prior beliefs. It defines independence through factorization of joint distributions. It then introduces continuous probability densities, their normalization and interval probabilities, transformation under changes of variables via the Jacobian, cumulative distribution functions, multivariate and mixed distributions, and the extension of probability rules to densities. Finally, it defines expectations as weighted averages for discrete and continuous distributions and begins discussing their estimation from samples.

nodes.title: 1.2.2 Expectations and covariances
nodes.summary: The text explains continuous and mixed probability distributions, normalization, and the extension of probability sum and product rules to densities, including an informal measure-theoretic justification. It then defines expectations for discrete, continuous, sampled, variable-specific, and conditional distributions, followed by variance and covariance for scalar and vector random variables, including their alternative formulas, interpretation, and the fact that independent variables have zero covariance.

nodes.title: 1.2.3 Bayesian probabilities
Thomas Bayes
nodes.summary: The text introduces Bayesian probability as a coherent framework for quantifying uncertainty, updating beliefs with evidence, and making decisions, contrasting it with frequentist probability based on repeatable events. It motivates probability through axiomatic extensions of Boolean logic, recounts the contributions of Bayes and Laplace, and develops Bayes’ theorem for inferring uncertain model parameters using priors, likelihoods, posteriors, and normalization. It contrasts Bayesian inference with maximum-likelihood estimation, error functions, and bootstrap-based frequentist uncertainty assessment; discusses the benefits and criticisms of priors, model comparison, and cross-validation; and reviews computational methods including Monte Carlo, variational Bayes, and expectation propagation. The section then begins an introduction to the Gaussian distribution, defining its density, parameters, positivity, and normalization, with a further biographical note on Laplace.

This section presents Bayesian probability as a logical and practical framework for representing uncertainty, revising beliefs with evidence, and making decisions. It covers the historical roles of Bayes and Laplace, derives Bayes’ theorem and its prior-likelihood-posterior structure, contrasts Bayesian methods with frequentist estimation and uncertainty analysis, examines priors, model comparison, and cross-validation, and surveys computational inference methods. It concludes by beginning the treatment of the Gaussian distribution and noting further biographical information about Laplace.

nodes.title: 1.2.4 The Gaussian distribution
nodes.summary: The text discusses the computational development of Bayesian methods, contrasting intensive Monte Carlo sampling with efficient deterministic approximations. It introduces the univariate and multivariate Gaussian distributions, explaining their parameters, normalization, moments, variance, mode, and geometric notation. For independent Gaussian data, it defines the likelihood and log likelihood, derives maximum likelihood estimates for the mean and variance, and explains the downward bias of the variance estimate, its unbiased correction, and its connection to overfitting and Bayesian approaches. Finally, it returns to polynomial curve fitting by modeling target values probabilistically with a Gaussian centered on the polynomial prediction and parameterized by a precision.

nodes.title: 1.2.5 Curve fitting re-visited
nodes.summary: The text explains the small-sample downward bias of maximum-likelihood Gaussian variance estimates, its reduction with larger datasets, and its connection to overfitting in complex models. It then reformulates polynomial curve fitting probabilistically by modeling targets with a Gaussian centered on the polynomial prediction. Independent-data likelihood maximization yields the usual sum-of-squares error for fitting coefficients and an estimate of the noise precision, while predictions become Gaussian distributions. Adding a Gaussian prior over coefficients produces a posterior whose maximum, or MAP estimate, is equivalent to regularized least squares. The text concludes by distinguishing MAP point estimation from fully Bayesian curve fitting, which requires integrating over all coefficient values.

nodes.title: 1.2.6 Bayesian curve fitting
nodes.summary: The text moves from maximum-likelihood polynomial regression to MAP and fully Bayesian curve fitting. It introduces a Gaussian prior over coefficients, shows that MAP estimation produces regularized least squares, and derives the Bayesian predictive distribution by integrating over the Gaussian posterior of the coefficients. The resulting predictive variance reflects both target noise and parameter uncertainty, illustrated for a ninth-order polynomial. It then introduces model selection, explaining how complexity affects generalization, why training error is inadequate because of overfitting, and how validation sets, test sets, and cross-validation are used to compare models, especially when data is limited.

This section develops probability theory for pattern recognition, beginning with random variables, probabilities, joint, marginal, conditional, sum, product, and Bayes’ rules, and extending them to independence, continuous and mixed probability densities, transformations, cumulative distributions, expectations, variance, and covariance. It presents Bayesian probability as a framework for updating beliefs and making decisions, contrasting it with frequentist methods and discussing priors, model comparison, cross-validation, and inference algorithms. The section then introduces Gaussian distributions and likelihood estimation, including variance bias and overfitting, before revisiting polynomial curve fitting probabilistically through maximum likelihood, MAP regularization, and fully Bayesian predictive distributions. It concludes with model complexity, generalization, validation, test sets, and cross-validation.

nodes.title: 1.3. Model Selection
nodes.summary: The text presents Bayesian polynomial predictive uncertainty and then discusses model selection. It explains how model complexity is controlled, why training performance is unreliable due to overfitting, and how validation, test sets, and S-fold or leave-one-out cross-validation can estimate generalization performance, along with their data and computational limitations. It introduces information criteria such as AIC and BIC as likelihood-based methods with complexity penalties, notes their tendency to favor overly simple models because they neglect parameter uncertainty, and motivates a fully Bayesian alternative. The text then transitions to the curse of dimensionality in higher-dimensional pattern-recognition spaces.

nodes.title: 1.4. The Curse of Dimensionality
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of model assessment by explaining S-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation, their computational and hyperparameter-search limitations, and information criteria such as AIC and BIC, noting their tendency to favor overly simple models and motivating Bayesian complexity control. It then introduces the curse of dimensionality through an oil-flow classification example and a cell-based classifier, showing that grid size grows exponentially, polynomial model parameters grow rapidly with dimensionality, and geometric intuition changes because volume and Gaussian probability concentrate near thin outer shells. Effective methods remain possible because real data often lie on lower-dimensional manifolds and vary smoothly. Finally, the text introduces decision theory, distinguishing probabilistic inference of p(x,t) from choosing optimal actions, illustrated by deciding whether to treat a patient based on an X-ray cancer classification.

nodes.title: 1.5. Decision Theory
1.5.1 Minimizing the misclassification rate
nodes.summary: The text introduces decision theory for classification, using Bayes’ theorem to relate priors, likelihoods, joint probabilities, and posterior class probabilities. It defines decision regions and boundaries, proves that minimizing the misclassification rate requires assigning each input to the class with the highest posterior probability, and extends this result from two to K classes, with a graphical illustration of the optimal boundary. It then explains expected-loss decision making for situations in which different errors have unequal consequences, defines loss matrices and their relation to utility, gives an asymmetric cancer-diagnosis example, and derives the rule of assigning each input to the class that minimizes posterior expected loss.

nodes.title: 1.5.2 Minimizing the expected loss
nodes.summary: The text explains decision-making under unequal classification costs. It introduces loss matrices using a cancer-diagnosis example, derives the rule of assigning each input to the class with minimum posterior expected loss, and contrasts loss minimization with utility maximization. It then presents the reject option, in which uncertain cases are withheld according to a posterior-probability threshold, discusses how the threshold controls rejection, and notes cost-sensitive rejection. Finally, it begins separating classification into inference, which estimates posterior probabilities from training data, and decision, which acts on them.

nodes.title: 1.5.3 The reject option
nodes.summary: The text explains minimum-expected-loss classification using posterior probabilities and introduces the reject option for uncertain cases. Inputs are rejected when their highest posterior probability does not exceed a threshold, with the threshold controlling how many cases are rejected; extreme threshold settings determine whether all or none are rejected. Rejection can also be incorporated into loss minimization through a loss matrix. A figure illustrates the reject region, and the text transitions to separating inference—learning posterior probabilities from training data—from the subsequent decision stage.

nodes.title: 1.5.4 Inference and decision
nodes.summary: The text explains decision-making from posterior probabilities, including minimum-loss classification and the reject option for uncertain cases. It contrasts generative, posterior-based discriminative, and direct discriminant-function approaches, discussing their complexity, data requirements, novelty detection capabilities, and the benefits of retaining posterior probabilities for changing losses, rejection, prior correction, and model combination. It presents naive Bayes combination of conditionally independent information sources and then extends decision theory to regression, showing that squared-error loss is minimized by the conditional mean.

nodes.title: 1.5.5 Loss functions for regression
nodes.summary: The text explains naive Bayes classification through conditional independence, posterior computation, class priors, normalization, and the limitations of factorizing only conditionals. It then develops regression decision theory, showing that squared-error loss is minimized by the conditional mean and decomposes into reducible prediction error plus irreducible conditional variance. It outlines joint-density, conditional-density, and direct-regression approaches, introduces Minkowski losses and their mean, median, and mode solutions, and begins information theory by defining information as surprise and motivating its logarithmic dependence on probability.

This section introduces decision theory as the process of converting probabilistic inference into optimal actions for classification and regression. It develops Bayes classification, decision regions, minimum-error and minimum-expected-loss rules, asymmetric costs, utilities, and rejection of uncertain cases. It distinguishes inference from decision and compares generative, posterior-based, and direct discriminative methods, including naive Bayes and its conditional-independence assumption. For regression, it derives the conditional mean under squared loss, explains reducible and irreducible error, and surveys density-based, direct-regression, and Minkowski-loss approaches. It concludes by beginning information theory through the notion of information as probabilistic surprise.

nodes.title: 1.6. Information Theory
Ludwig Boltzmann
nodes.summary: The text develops continuous entropy by taking the zero-bin-width limit of discrete entropy, defining differential entropy and explaining its divergence-related distinction from discrete entropy. It derives, under normalization, mean, and variance constraints, that the maximum-entropy continuous distribution is Gaussian, gives its entropy, and notes that differential entropy may be negative. It then defines conditional entropy and states the entropy chain rule. The section introduces relative entropy/Kullback–Leibler divergence as the excess coding cost of using an approximate distribution, notes its asymmetry and nonnegativity, and begins its proof via convex functions. Biographical sidebars discuss Boltzmann’s statistical interpretation of thermodynamic entropy and Shannon’s foundational role in information theory.

nodes.title: 1.6.1 Relative entropy and mutual information
Claude Shannon

nodes.summary: The text explains mutual information as the Bayesian reduction in uncertainty produced by observing another variable, then presents exercises on deriving normal equations for polynomial least-squares fitting, extending them to regularized fitting, applying conditional probability to a box-and-fruit problem, analyzing how probability-density maxima change under nonlinear and linear variable transformations, and proving a variance identity for a function f(x).

nodes.title: 1.6 () Show that if two variables x and y are independent, then their covariance is zero.
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 1.6–1.11 on covariance and independence, Gaussian normalization and related identities, Gaussian modes, means and variances of sums of independent variables, and verification of maximum-likelihood results by differentiating the log likelihood.

nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on covariance and independence, normalization and key identities of univariate Gaussian distributions, Gaussian modes in one and multiple dimensions, means and variances of sums of independent variables, and deriving Gaussian parameter estimates by maximizing the log likelihood.

nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on covariance and independence, evaluation and normalization of the Gaussian integral, verification of Gaussian distribution identities through variable changes and differentiation, identification of Gaussian modes, mean and variance rules for sums of independent variables, and derivation of Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimates by optimizing the log likelihood.

nodes.title: 1.12 ( ) www Using the results (1.49) and (1.50), show that
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 1.12–1.41 from an introductory chapter, covering Gaussian moments and unbiased variance estimation; symmetric and antisymmetric matrix decompositions; counting polynomial parameters and their asymptotic growth; Gamma-function identities; hypersphere geometry and high-dimensional volume concentration; radial behavior of high-dimensional Gaussians; Bayes classification, loss matrices, rejection, and regression under different losses; entropy, Jensen’s inequality, maximum-entropy Gaussians, KL divergence, conditional and differential entropy, linear transformations, mutual information, convexity, and arithmetic–geometric mean inequalities. It also includes a binary-distribution exercise requiring computation of marginal, conditional, joint entropy, and mutual information and visualization of their relationships.

This section introduces Shannon and the foundations of information theory, developing conditional entropy, convexity and Jensen’s inequality, KL divergence, and mutual information, with their interpretations in coding, density estimation, independence, and maximum likelihood. Its exercises broadly reinforce probability, covariance, Gaussian distributions, estimation, least squares, transformations, matrices, special functions, high-dimensional geometry, Bayesian decision-making, regression, entropy, and mutual information.

This section introduces Shannon’s information theory and develops conditional entropy, convexity with Jensen’s inequality, KL divergence, and mutual information, emphasizing their roles in coding, density estimation, independence, and maximum likelihood. Exercises reinforce these ideas alongside probability, statistical estimation, Gaussian models, linear algebra, geometry, Bayesian decision-making, regression, entropy, and mutual information.

The section briefly concludes the discussion of regression with Minkowski loss, then introduces information theory through information content, entropy, coding, and the interpretation of entropy as uncertainty or disorder. It extends these ideas to differential and conditional entropy, derives the maximum-entropy Gaussian, and develops KL divergence and mutual information, emphasizing their mathematical properties and applications to coding, density estimation, independence, and likelihood. Historical notes on Boltzmann and Shannon and a broad set of related exercises complete the section.

The introduction surveys pattern recognition and machine learning through handwritten-digit recognition, emphasizing training, testing, generalization, preprocessing, feature extraction, and dimensionality reduction. It distinguishes supervised classification and regression, unsupervised clustering, density estimation and visualization, and reinforcement learning with its reward, credit-assignment, and exploration–exploitation challenges. Polynomial curve fitting illustrates least-squares learning, model complexity, underfitting, overfitting, regularization, validation, and probabilistic prediction. The section develops probability theory and Bayesian inference, including distributions, expectations, Gaussian models, likelihood, MAP and fully Bayesian prediction, then covers model selection using validation, cross-validation, information criteria, and Bayesian complexity control. It explains the curse of dimensionality and lower-dimensional data structure, introduces decision theory for converting inference into cost-sensitive classification and regression actions, and concludes with information theory, including coding, entropy, differential and conditional entropy, KL divergence, and mutual information.

nodes.title: 2 Probability Distributions
2.1. Binary Variables
2.1.1 The beta distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the mean and variance of the binomial distribution, then develops Bayesian inference for a Bernoulli/binomial parameter using the conjugate beta prior. It gives the beta distribution’s normalization, moments, interpretation, and illustrative shapes; derives the beta posterior and explains hyperparameters as effective counts; describes sequential updating, predictive probabilities, convergence to maximum likelihood, and posterior concentration. It also presents general identities showing that the average posterior mean equals the prior mean and that average posterior uncertainty decreases, while noting exceptions for individual data sets. Finally, it begins the transition from binary to multinomial variables represented with a 1-of-K encoding and includes several exercise and section references.

The section introduces binary variables through the Bernoulli distribution, deriving its moments, the likelihood and sufficient statistic for observed data, and the maximum-likelihood estimate, while highlighting overfitting from limited samples. It then develops the binomial distribution for counts of successes, including its combinatorial form and moments, and presents Bayesian estimation with the conjugate beta prior: its properties, posterior updating, effective-count interpretation, predictions, convergence, and uncertainty behavior. The section concludes by starting the extension to multinomial variables with 1-of-K representations and includes illustrative figures, exercises, references, and a note on Jacob Bernoulli.

nodes.title: 2.2. Multinomial Variables
2.2.1 The Dirichlet distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the multinomial maximum-likelihood estimate and defines the multinomial distribution and count constraint. It introduces the Dirichlet distribution as the multinomial’s conjugate prior, describes its simplex domain, normalization, parameter interpretation, posterior update, and illustrative shapes, and notes the binomial/beta correspondence for two states. A sidebar presents biographical information about Dirichlet. The text then begins the Gaussian-distribution section, giving scalar and multivariate formulas and explaining its roles in maximum entropy and the central limit theorem.

This section introduces the 1-of-K representation and multinomial distribution for K-state discrete variables, establishes its normalization and mean, and derives the likelihood, sufficient outcome counts, and constrained maximum-likelihood estimates. It then develops the Dirichlet conjugate prior, its simplex geometry, normalization, interpretation, posterior update, shapes, and reduction to the beta distribution for two outcomes, with a biographical note on Dirichlet. The section concludes by beginning the treatment of Gaussian distributions and their roles in maximum entropy and the central limit theorem, while also placing the discussion in the context of Bayesian uncertainty reduction.

nodes.title: 2.3. The Gaussian Distribution
nodes.summary: The text transitions from Dirichlet and binary/multinomial representations to an introduction of the one- and multidimensional Gaussian distributions, specifying their parameters and formulas. It explains their emergence from maximum-entropy principles and the central limit theorem, illustrating convergence with averages of uniform variables and the binomial distribution. It previews a technically detailed treatment of Gaussian geometry and matrix identities, and includes a biographical sidebar on Carl Friedrich Gauss and his mathematical contributions.

This section introduces probability distributions as fundamental components of pattern-recognition models and as simple settings for studying density estimation, Bayesian inference, and statistical uncertainty, assuming independent and identically distributed data. It develops Bernoulli and binomial models, including their moments, likelihoods, sufficient statistics, maximum-likelihood estimation, overfitting, and beta-prior Bayesian estimation. It then extends these ideas to 1-of-K and multinomial variables, deriving their normalization, means, likelihoods, constrained estimates, and Dirichlet conjugate priors, including simplex geometry, posterior updating, and the beta special case. Finally, it introduces one- and multidimensional Gaussian distributions, explaining their emergence from maximum entropy and the central limit theorem, with examples of convergence, a preview of Gaussian geometry and matrix methods, and supplementary biographies, figures, exercises, and references.

nodes.title: Appendix C
Carl Friedrich Gauss
nodes.summary: The text explains why Gaussian distributions arise as limits of averages and binomial variables, then develops their geometry, normalization, and moments using covariance-matrix eigendecomposition. Mahalanobis-distance contours are ellipsoids determined by covariance eigenvectors and eigenvalues, and an orthogonal coordinate transformation factorizes the multivariate Gaussian into independent univariate Gaussians. It establishes that μ and Σ are respectively the mean and covariance, discusses parameter-count and modeling limitations of full, diagonal, and isotropic covariance matrices, and motivates latent-variable and structured graphical models. Finally, it introduces conditional Gaussian distributions by partitioning variables, means, covariance, and precision matrices, preparing the derivation of Gaussian conditionals and marginals.

nodes.title: 2.3.1 Conditional Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text develops the conditional distribution of one subset of variables in a partitioned multivariate Gaussian. After defining partitions of the vector, mean, covariance, and precision matrices, it uses the quadratic exponent and completing-the-square argument to show that the conditional distribution is Gaussian. Its mean and covariance are first derived in precision form, then rewritten using a partitioned-matrix inverse and Schur complement in covariance form. The conditional mean is linear in the observed variables, the covariance is constant with respect to them, and the result provides an example of a linear-Gaussian model.

nodes.title: 2.3.2 Marginal Gaussian distributions
nodes.summary: The text derives the marginal distribution of a subset of variables in a partitioned multivariate Gaussian by completing the square in the variables being integrated out. The marginal has mean μa and covariance given initially by the inverse Schur complement of the precision matrix, which is shown via block-matrix identities to equal the covariance block Σaa. It summarizes the conditional and marginal Gaussian formulas, contrasts the roles of covariance and precision matrices, illustrates the results with a bivariate-Gaussian figure, and begins introducing Bayes’ theorem for Gaussian variables with a linear-mean, constant-covariance conditional distribution.

nodes.title: 2.3.3 Bayes’ theorem for Gaussian variables
nodes.summary: The text illustrates marginal and conditional distributions of a multivariate Gaussian, then derives Bayes’ theorem for a linear Gaussian model. It constructs the joint Gaussian, its precision, covariance, and mean, and obtains the marginal distribution of y and posterior distribution of x given y, including Gaussian convolution as a special case. It concludes with maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian, identifying the sufficient statistics and deriving the sample-mean estimate of the mean.

nodes.title: 2.3.4 Maximum likelihood for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text derives the marginal and conditional distributions associated with Gaussian marginal and conditional models, then develops maximum-likelihood estimation for a multivariate Gaussian. It presents the log likelihood and its sufficient statistics, derives the sample mean and covariance estimators, analyzes their expectations and the covariance estimator’s bias, and gives the unbiased covariance correction. It concludes by introducing sequential maximum-likelihood estimation, motivated by online processing and very large data sets.

nodes.title: 2.3.5 Sequential estimation
nodes.summary: The text derives the ML covariance estimate for a multivariate Gaussian, establishes that the mean estimate is unbiased while the covariance estimate is biased downward, and gives the unbiased N/(N−1) correction. It then introduces sequential estimation, deriving the recursive Gaussian mean update and presenting the Robbins–Monro stochastic root-finding algorithm, its assumptions, step-size conditions, convergence rationale, and application to general ML estimation and Gaussian means. Finally, it begins Bayesian Gaussian inference for an unknown mean with known variance by specifying the likelihood and noting its quadratic form and the use of a Gaussian prior.

nodes.title: 2.3.6 Bayesian inference for the Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of Gaussian sequential estimation and develops Bayesian inference for Gaussian parameters. It explains the linear regression-function interpretation of Gaussian maximum likelihood, sequential mean updates, and their multivariate extension. It then derives Gaussian conjugate posteriors for an unknown mean with known variance, emphasizing precision-weighted updating, sequential Bayes inference, limiting behavior, and graphical illustration. For unknown variance it introduces precision and the gamma conjugate prior, derives posterior parameters and effective-observation interpretations, and notes the inverse-gamma alternative. It derives the normal-gamma prior for jointly unknown mean and precision, then generalizes to multivariate Gaussian models using Gaussian, Wishart, inverse-Wishart, and normal-Wishart distributions. Finally, it begins introducing Student’s t-distribution as the result of integrating out Gaussian precision under a gamma prior.

nodes.title: 2.3.7 Student’s t-distribution
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of Gaussian conjugate priors by introducing the Wishart prior for an unknown multivariate precision matrix, the inverse Wishart alternative for covariance matrices, and the normal-Wishart prior when both mean and precision are unknown. It then derives Student’s t-distribution by integrating a Gaussian precision under a gamma prior, explains its parameterization, Gaussian and Cauchy limiting cases, infinite-Gaussian-mixture interpretation, heavy tails, and robustness to outliers, including graphical illustrations and implications for regression. The multivariate t-distribution is obtained through an analogous Gamma mixture, with its density, Mahalanobis-distance form, mean, covariance, and mode stated. Finally, the text introduces periodic variables, explains why ordinary Gaussian modeling is coordinate-dependent for angular data, and begins an invariant approach by representing angles as unit vectors on the circle and averaging those vectors.

nodes.title: 2.3.8 Periodic variables
nodes.summary: The text first gives the multivariate Student’s t-distribution, its Mahalanobis-distance form, and its mean, covariance, and mode conditions. It then explains why ordinary Gaussians are unsuitable for periodic variables and develops a coordinate-invariant circular mean using unit vectors. The von Mises, or circular normal, distribution is derived by conditioning an isotropic two-dimensional Gaussian on the unit circle; its parameters, Bessel-function normalization, Gaussian approximation, and maximum-likelihood estimators are presented. Alternative periodic modeling methods and von Mises mixtures for multimodal data are discussed. Finally, the text introduces Gaussian mixtures through the Old Faithful example, showing why mixtures capture clustered data better than a single Gaussian.

nodes.title: 2.3.9 Mixtures of Gaussians
nodes.summary: The text transitions from periodic distributions to Gaussian mixture models and the exponential family. It reviews limitations and alternatives to the von Mises distribution, then uses the bimodal Old Faithful data to motivate mixtures of Gaussians, defining their density, component parameters, mixing-coefficient constraints, latent-variable interpretation, responsibilities, and maximum-likelihood estimation difficulties. It then introduces the general exponential-family form and demonstrates that the Bernoulli distribution is a member, with its natural parameter expressed as the log odds.

nodes.title: 2.4. The Exponential Family
2.4.1 Maximum likelihood and sufficient statistics
nodes.summary: The text develops maximum likelihood, sufficient statistics, and conjugate priors for exponential-family distributions. It presents the Gaussian in exponential-family form, derives moments from derivatives of the normalization function, and shows that ML estimation depends only on summed sufficient statistics, with examples for Bernoulli and Gaussian distributions and consistency as the sample size grows. It then introduces the general conjugate prior, demonstrates that the posterior preserves the prior’s functional form, and interprets its hyperparameter as an effective number of pseudo-observations. Finally, it begins discussing noninformative priors and how prior zero probabilities persist in the posterior.

nodes.title: 2.4.2 Conjugate priors
nodes.summary: The text explains that exponential-family maximum-likelihood estimates depend on data only through sufficient statistics, illustrating this with Bernoulli and Gaussian distributions, and notes consistency as the sample size grows, as well as the analogous Bayesian sufficiency property. It then defines conjugate priors, gives examples and the general exponential-family form, demonstrates that the posterior preserves the prior’s functional form, and interprets the prior-strength parameter as a number of pseudo-observations. Finally, it begins discussing noninformative priors, noting that values excluded by the prior remain excluded from the posterior.

nodes.title: 2.4.3 Noninformative priors
nodes.summary: The text explains sufficient statistics and their role in maximum-likelihood and Bayesian inference for exponential-family distributions, including consistency as sample size grows and examples for Bernoulli and Gaussian models. It derives the general form and interpretation of conjugate priors, then discusses noninformative priors, including improper uniform, location-invariant, and scale-invariant priors, their dependence on parameterization, and their Gaussian mean, variance, and precision examples. It concludes by introducing nonparametric density estimation as an alternative to restrictive parametric models and describes normalized histogram density estimation.

The section introduces the exponential family as a general framework encompassing distributions such as Bernoulli, multinomial, and Gaussian models, develops their natural-parameter, normalization, and sufficient-statistic representations, and derives sigmoid and softmax forms. It explains how normalization derivatives yield moments and how maximum-likelihood and Bayesian inference depend on data through sufficient statistics, including consistency and examples. The section then develops conjugate priors and their pseudo-observation interpretation, discusses noninformative and invariant priors and their parameterization issues, and concludes by introducing nonparametric density estimation with normalized histograms. It also contrasts these analytic properties with Gaussian-mixture likelihoods, which require numerical optimization or expectation maximization.

nodes.title: 2.5. Nonparametric Methods
2.5.1 Kernel density estimators
nodes.summary: The text introduces kernel and nearest-neighbour nonparametric density estimation as improvements over histograms. Starting from binomial statistics for the number of samples in a local region, it derives the estimate p(x) = K/(NV), highlighting the need to balance local uniformity against having enough observations. Kernel estimation fixes the region volume, uses a hypercube or smoother kernel such as a Gaussian, and averages kernel contributions from all data points. Its bandwidth controls the trade-off between noise and oversmoothing, and valid kernels must be nonnegative and normalized. Parzen estimators require only data storage during training but have evaluation cost linear in dataset size. Nearest-neighbour estimation instead fixes the number of included points and adapts the region volume to local density, addressing the limitations of a globally fixed kernel width; convergence conditions for both methods are also stated.

nodes.title: 2.5.2 Nearest-neighbour methods
nodes.summary: The text compares kernel and nearest-neighbour nonparametric density estimation. Kernel density estimators use a bandwidth h, whose small-to-large trade-off controls noise versus oversmoothing; valid kernels are nonnegative and integrate to one. They require only storage during training but have evaluation costs linear in the data size. K-nearest-neighbour density estimation instead fixes the number K of enclosed points and adapts the volume to local density, with K controlling smoothness, although the resulting estimate is not globally integrable. The method extends to classification: a sphere containing K total points yields class counts K_k, and Bayes' theorem reduces posterior comparison to choosing the class with the largest K_k. The text discusses the K = 1 rule, its geometric decision boundaries, oil-flow classification examples, and its asymptotic error bound. Storage and search costs can be mitigated with tree structures, but the limitations of nonparametric methods and restricted parametric models motivate more flexible, complexity-controlled models. The section concludes with exercises on Bernoulli moments and entropy, the {-1, 1} Bernoulli form, and proving binomial normalization via a combinations identity.

This section introduces nonparametric density estimation as a flexible alternative to potentially misspecified parametric distributions. It develops histogram methods, including their normalization, bandwidth and edge effects, practical benefits, discontinuities, and curse-of-dimensionality limitations, then motivates local methods. Kernel estimators use fixed neighborhoods and bandwidth-controlled smoothing, while nearest-neighbour estimators adapt neighborhood volume to local density; both involve convergence and computational trade-offs. Nearest-neighbour methods are also applied to classification through class counts, including the 1-nearest-neighbour rule, geometric boundaries, examples, error bounds, and efficient search structures. The section closes by motivating complexity-controlled flexible models and assigning exercises on Bernoulli distributions, entropy, and binomial normalization.

nodes.summary: The passage discusses the asymptotic error guarantee of 1-nearest-neighbour classification, the storage and computational drawbacks of nearest-neighbour and kernel-density methods, and the use of tree-based searches to improve efficiency. It contrasts the limitations of nonparametric methods with those of simple parametric models and motivates flexible density models with independently controllable complexity. The exercises cover Bernoulli-distribution moments and entropy, an alternative {-1,1} Bernoulli representation and its properties, and a combinatorial identity used to prove binomial-distribution normalization.

nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of nearest-neighbour, kernel, tree-search, nonparametric, and parametric density models, motivating flexible models with independently controllable complexity. nodes.title: 3 Linear Models for Regression
3.1. Linear Basis Function Models
3.1.1 Maximum likelihood and least squares
nodes.summary: The text introduces linear basis-function regression and basis examples, then develops its Gaussian maximum-likelihood interpretation. It derives the likelihood, least-squares error, normal-equation solution, design matrix and pseudoinverse, bias estimate, and noise-precision estimate. It also explains least squares geometrically as projection onto the span of the basis vectors, discusses numerical problems caused by near-collinearity and remedies using SVD or regularization, and introduces sequential learning as an alternative to processing large data sets in one batch.

nodes.title: 3.1.2 Geometry of least squares
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometric interpretation of linear least-squares regression: data and basis functions are represented as vectors, predictions lie in the subspace spanned by the basis vectors, and the least-squares solution is the orthogonal projection of the target vector onto that subspace. It notes that residual variance determines the inverse noise precision, discusses numerical instability caused by singular or nearly singular design matrices, and identifies SVD and regularization as remedies. It then introduces sequential or online learning as a computationally efficient alternative to batch learning for large data sets.

nodes.title: 3.1.3 Sequential learning
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometric interpretation of least squares as the orthogonal projection of the target vector onto the subspace spanned by evaluated basis functions, and notes that residual variance determines inverse noise precision. It discusses numerical instability in normal-equation solutions caused by nearly dependent basis vectors, with SVD and regularization as remedies. It then introduces sequential or online learning through stochastic gradient descent and derives the LMS update, emphasizing careful learning-rate selection. Finally, it presents regularized least squares using an L2 weight penalty, explaining its role in preventing overfitting and its interpretations as weight decay and parameter shrinkage.

nodes.title: 3.1.4 Regularized least squares
nodes.summary: The text introduces sequential learning through stochastic gradient descent and derives the LMS update for sum-of-squares regression. It then develops regularized least squares, explaining quadratic weight decay, its closed-form solution, generalized ℓ_q penalties, and the lasso’s sparse solutions through constrained optimization. Regularization controls over-fitting and effective model complexity, though λ must be selected; the discussion subsequently focuses on the quadratic case. Finally, it extends linear basis-function regression to multiple outputs using a shared basis-function matrix, an isotropic Gaussian target distribution, and the resulting matrix-based log likelihood.

nodes.title: 3.1.5 Multiple outputs
nodes.summary: The text concludes the regularization discussion by contrasting quadratic and lasso constraints, noting that lasso produces sparse solutions and that the chapter will focus on quadratic regularization. It then extends linear regression to multiple target variables using a shared basis-function matrix and an isotropic Gaussian likelihood, derives the matrix maximum-likelihood solution, and shows that each output can be fitted independently using a common pseudoinverse; this remains true for arbitrary Gaussian covariance because the parameters determine only the mean. The discussion returns to one target and introduces bias-variance and model complexity: maximum-likelihood or least-squares fitting can overfit complex models on small data sets, while restricting basis functions reduces flexibility. Regularization helps control overfitting but requires choosing lambda, which cannot be learned by jointly minimizing the regularized objective because that yields lambda = 0. Bayesian parameter marginalization avoids this issue, while the text first develops the frequentist bias-variance trade-off and relates it to regression decision theory and loss functions.

This section develops linear basis-function regression, in which predictions are linear in adjustable parameters but may be nonlinear in the inputs through polynomial, spline, Gaussian, sigmoidal, Fourier, or wavelet features. It derives least-squares regression from a Gaussian maximum-likelihood model, including normal-equation, design-matrix, pseudoinverse, bias, and noise-precision results, and interprets the solution geometrically as projection onto the basis-function subspace. It addresses ill-conditioned or dependent bases using SVD and regularization, then presents sequential stochastic-gradient/LMS learning for large data sets. Regularized least squares is developed through quadratic weight decay and general ℓq penalties, including sparse lasso solutions and the need to choose the regularization strength. The framework is extended to multiple outputs with shared bases and Gaussian likelihoods. Finally, the section discusses model complexity, overfitting, bias-variance trade-offs, loss-based decision theory, and why Bayesian parameter marginalization can address the difficulty of selecting regularization by joint optimization.

nodes.title: 3.2. The Bias-Variance Decomposition
nodes.summary: The text first derives the shared pseudoinverse solution for multiple-target linear regression and explains why the target regressions decouple. It then introduces the frequentist bias-variance decomposition: expected squared prediction loss consists of squared bias, variance, and irreducible noise. Bias measures systematic deviation of the ensemble-average prediction from the true conditional mean, while variance measures sensitivity to the training data. Flexible and rigid models trade low bias for high variance and vice versa. A sinusoidal experiment with Gaussian basis functions demonstrates how regularization controls this trade-off, identifies a near-optimal λ, and shows that averaging fits can improve predictions. The section notes the decomposition's limited practical usefulness with only one data set and motivates Bayesian linear regression as a principled approach to avoiding overfitting and selecting model complexity. It begins that treatment by specifying a Gaussian prior over weights, conjugate to the quadratic likelihood when the noise precision is known.

nodes.title: 3.3. Bayesian Linear Regression
3.3.1 Parameter distribution
nodes.summary: The text transitions from the limitations of frequentist bias-variance analysis and hold-out validation to Bayesian linear regression as a way to control overfitting and infer model complexity from training data. It derives Gaussian posterior weight distributions from Gaussian priors and the linear-regression likelihood, explains MAP estimation, limiting cases, sequential updating, and the connection between Gaussian priors and quadratic regularization. A synthetic straight-line example illustrates how likelihoods and posteriors become increasingly concentrated as data arrive. It also discusses non-Gaussian exponential-power priors and derives the Gaussian predictive distribution, whose uncertainty combines observation noise with parameter uncertainty that decreases as more data are observed.

nodes.title: 3.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text generalizes the weight prior beyond the Gaussian case, relates posterior maximization to regularized regression, and derives the Gaussian predictive distribution for Bayesian linear regression, separating noise from parameter uncertainty and explaining how additional data reduce predictive variance. It illustrates these ideas with sinusoidal-data plots and posterior function samples, discusses overconfident extrapolation with localized bases and alternatives involving Gaussian processes or Student's t prediction, and develops the equivalent-kernel interpretation in which predictions are localized weighted sums of training targets.

nodes.title: 3.3.3 Equivalent kernel
nodes.summary: The text explains the equivalent kernel in Bayesian linear regression: the predictive mean is a linear combination of training targets whose input-dependent weights are determined by k(x,x') = beta phi(x)^T S_N phi(x'). These weights are typically localized around the prediction point, even for nonlocal polynomial and sigmoidal bases, and the same kernel determines covariance and joint predictive uncertainty. This motivates direct-kernel methods such as Gaussian processes. The kernel weights sum to one under stated basis and data assumptions, though they can be negative, and the kernel can be represented as an inner product in a transformed feature space. The text then introduces Bayesian model comparison, emphasizing marginalization over parameters to reduce overfitting, compare models directly on training data without cross-validation, and learn multiple complexity parameters jointly. Model uncertainty is represented by priors and posteriors over models, with posterior probability proportional to prior probability times the model evidence.

Bayesian linear regression is developed as a probabilistic framework for controlling overfitting, learning model complexity, and quantifying uncertainty. The section derives weight posteriors and predictive distributions for Gaussian and more general priors, explains MAP estimation, regularization, sequential updating, and the separate effects of noise and parameter uncertainty, and illustrates these ideas with synthetic and sinusoidal examples. It then interprets predictions through the equivalent kernel, covering localized and potentially negative training-point weights, predictive covariance, feature-space representations, Gaussian-process connections, and extrapolation limitations. Finally, it introduces Bayesian model comparison through parameter marginalization, model evidence, and posterior model probabilities, enabling direct comparison and joint learning of model complexities without cross-validation.

nodes.title: 3.4. Bayesian Model Comparison
nodes.summary: The text concludes the equivalent-kernel discussion by noting that the kernel may be signed and has a nonlinear inner-product representation. It then develops Bayesian model comparison: posterior model probabilities combine model priors with marginal likelihoods, whose ratios are Bayes factors; predictions can average all models or select the most probable one. The evidence integrates over parameter uncertainty and balances maximum fit against an Occam complexity penalty, favoring models of intermediate complexity and, when the true model is included, favoring it on average through the KL-divergence property. The method avoids overfitting and validation-based comparison but depends strongly on valid, proper priors and model assumptions, so independent testing remains advisable. Finally, the evidence approximation for linear regression is introduced, fixing hyperparameters α and β at marginal-likelihood-maximizing values instead of fully integrating over them, while retaining integration over the weights.

nodes.title: 3.5. The Evidence Approximation
3.5.1 Evaluation of the evidence function
nodes.summary: The text introduces the evidence framework for estimating the hyperparameters α and β in Bayesian linear regression, explaining its relationship to regularization, alternatives involving Gamma priors and Laplace approximation, and its equivalence with EM optimization. It evaluates the marginal likelihood by integrating over weights, completing the square using the Hessian A and posterior mean m_N, and derives the closed-form log-evidence expression. A polynomial-regression example illustrates how evidence trades fit against complexity and selects the cubic model. Finally, it begins maximizing the evidence with respect to α by diagonalizing βΦᵀΦ and deriving the corresponding stationary-point equation.

nodes.title: 3.5.2 Maximizing the evidence function
nodes.summary: The text explains why Bayesian model evidence selects a cubic polynomial as the best balance between fit and complexity, then derives iterative evidence-maximization updates for the prior precision α and noise precision β using the eigenvalues of βΦ^TΦ and the effective parameter count γ. It emphasizes that α can be learned from training data without validation data. Geometric interpretation shows how the prior shrinks weakly supported parameter directions while preserving well-determined ones. The quantity γ measures the effective number of parameters, and the Bayesian noise-variance estimate uses N − γ rather than N degrees of freedom.

nodes.title: 3.5.3 Effective number of parameters
nodes.summary: The text explains the effective number of parameters in Bayesian linear regression through the Hessian eigenvalue decomposition. The prior shrinks weakly data-constrained parameter directions toward zero, while strongly constrained directions remain near their maximum-likelihood values; the resulting effective parameter count gamma ranges from zero to M. This count replaces the nominal number of fitted parameters in the Bayesian variance estimate, correcting maximum-likelihood bias analogously to the N - 1 correction for estimating a Gaussian mean. A sinusoidal-data example demonstrates evidence-based selection of alpha, its relationship to gamma, the evidence maximum, and generalization performance, as well as the effect of alpha on individual weights. In the large-data limit, gamma equals M and simplified re-estimation formulas for alpha and beta result. The section concludes by introducing limitations of fixed basis-function models despite their analytical and Bayesian advantages.

This section introduces the evidence approximation, in which hyperparameters α and β in Bayesian linear regression are selected by maximizing the marginal likelihood rather than fully marginalized. It explains the predictive approximation, derives and evaluates the closed-form evidence, and shows how evidence balances fit and complexity to select models. Iterative updates for α and β, their geometric interpretation, and the effective parameter count γ are developed, including the corrected N − γ noise estimate and large-data limits. Examples with polynomial and sinusoidal regression illustrate model selection, regularization, evidence, and generalization. The section also discusses prior sensitivity, improper-prior caveats, the need for independent testing, and limitations of fixed basis-function models.

nodes.title: 3.6. Limitations of Fixed Basis Functions
nodes.summary: The text reports how Bayesian evidence selects the regularization parameter by the intersection of γ and 2αE_W, confirms that the evidence peak aligns with this intersection and near-optimal generalization, and illustrates how the effective parameter count changes with α. It then explains the benefits and limitations of fixed-basis linear models, emphasizing the curse of dimensionality and describing how data manifolds, localized basis functions, adaptive neural-network bases, and relevant input directions alleviate the problem. The exercise establishes the relationship between logistic sigmoid and tanh functions and asks for the corresponding coefficient transformation.
