This section introduces linear regression for supervised prediction, emphasizing models that are linear in parameters while using nonlinear fixed basis functions of the inputs. It develops least-squares and Gaussian maximum-likelihood regression, projection geometry, numerical stability, stochastic learning, regularization and sparsity, multivariate outputs, and model-complexity issues. It explains bias-variance behavior and overfitting, then presents Bayesian linear regression, including posterior and predictive uncertainty, sequential learning, equivalent kernels, Gaussian-process connections, and extrapolation. Bayesian model comparison and the evidence approximation show how marginal likelihood, Occam factors, effective parameter counts, and hyperparameter re-estimation can select complexity without cross-validation, while also exposing prior and model-assumption limitations. The section concludes with the curse of dimensionality and adaptive alternatives, and exercises covering the chapter’s geometric, probabilistic, Bayesian, predictive, kernel, conjugacy, and evidence derivations.

nodes.title: 4 Linear Models for Classification
4.1. Discriminant Functions
4.1.1 Two classes
nodes.summary: The text introduces linear discriminant functions for classification, noting the greater complexity caused by nonlinear parameter dependence and the applicability of fixed basis-function transformations. It defines binary linear discriminants, explains their geometric interpretation—including the roles of the weight vector and bias, the hyperplane decision boundary, and signed distance—then presents an augmented-vector notation. Finally, it begins the multiclass case and identifies problems with constructing K-class classifiers through one-versus-the-rest binary classifiers.

nodes.title: 4.1.2 Multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text explains the geometry and signed-distance interpretation of binary linear discriminants, including an augmented-vector notation that turns the bias into an additional parameter. It then examines multiclass classification, showing why one-versus-the-rest and one-versus-one combinations of binary classifiers can create ambiguous regions, and presents a unified K-function linear discriminant whose pairwise boundaries are hyperplanes. Its decision regions are proven to be singly connected and convex. Finally, it introduces least squares, Fisher’s linear discriminant, and the perceptron as learning methods, beginning with least-squares classification using 1-of-K targets, while noting that linear least-squares outputs may poorly estimate posterior probabilities and fall outside the valid probability range.

nodes.title: 4.1.3 Least squares for classification
nodes.summary: The text establishes that multiclass linear-discriminant decision regions are convex and singly connected, notes the equivalence of two- and single-discriminant formulations for binary classification, and introduces least squares, Fisher’s discriminant, and the perceptron as parameter-learning methods. It develops least-squares classification using one-of-K targets, augmented matrix notation, and a pseudoinverse closed-form solution; explains preservation of target-sum constraints; and emphasizes that outputs are not necessarily probabilities. It also details least squares’ sensitivity to outliers and poor performance on multiclass data, illustrated against logistic regression, attributing these weaknesses to its inappropriate Gaussian assumption before beginning the discussion of Fisher’s linear discriminant.

nodes.title: 4.1.4 Fisher’s linear discriminant
nodes.summary: The text contrasts least-squares and logistic-regression classification, highlighting least squares’ sensitivity to outliers and its poor performance on multiclass data because of its inappropriate Gaussian modeling assumption. It then introduces Fisher’s linear discriminant as a one-dimensional projection method that maximizes class-mean separation relative to within-class variation. The Fisher criterion leads to the projection direction w proportional to S_W^{-1}(m_2 − m_1), with the class means, covariance matrices, threshold classification, and optional Gaussian modeling of projected classes discussed. Finally, it begins explaining the relationship between Fisher’s discriminant and least-squares classification through alternative target coding.

nodes.title: 4.1.5 Relation to least squares
nodes.summary: The text derives Fisher’s linear discriminant by maximizing the ratio of between-class to within-class projected variance, obtaining the projection direction w proportional to S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1). It explains the isotropic-covariance special case, distinguishes the projection from the subsequent threshold-based discriminant, and discusses Gaussian modeling of projected classes and threshold selection. It then shows that, with specially chosen two-class least-squares targets, the normal equations yield the same Fisher weight direction, along with the bias w0 = -w^T m; consequently, classification can be performed using w^T(x - m) with threshold zero.

nodes.title: 4.1.6 Fisher’s discriminant for multiple classes
nodes.summary: The text generalizes Fisher’s discriminant to multiple classes by projecting inputs into several linear features and defining within-class, total, and between-class covariance matrices in both the original and projected spaces. It proposes maximizing the trace ratio of between-class to within-class covariance, solved using the leading eigenvectors of S_W^{-1}S_B. Because the between-class covariance has rank at most K − 1, Fisher’s method can produce no more than K − 1 informative linear features. The section then introduces the perceptron as a two-class generalized linear discriminant using a fixed nonlinear feature transformation.

nodes.title: 4.1.7 The perceptron algorithm
Frank Rosenblatt
nodes.summary: This section explains the perceptron’s step-function model, ±1 target coding, perceptron criterion, and stochastic gradient-descent learning rule, including how misclassified examples update the weights. It discusses why total misclassification count is unsuitable for gradient optimization, analyzes update effects, and states the convergence theorem and its limitations on separable and nonseparable data. Historical material covers Rosenblatt, criticism of perceptrons, and the Mark 1 hardware, while figures illustrate learning convergence and analogue implementation. The section also notes limitations in probabilistic outputs, multiclass use, and fixed-basis linearity, introduces the related adaline, and transitions to probabilistic generative classification models.

The section first completes the discussion of projected within- and between-class covariance criteria, their eigenvector solution, and the limit of K−1 discriminative features. It then presents Rosenblatt’s two-class perceptron using fixed nonlinear features and a step-function output, explaining target coding, the perceptron loss, stochastic updates for misclassified examples, optimization considerations, convergence on separable data, and failure to achieve a separating solution otherwise. Historical developments, hardware implementation, and illustrative convergence and analogue figures are included, followed by limitations concerning probabilities, multiclass classification, and fixed-basis linearity, an introduction to adaline, and a transition to probabilistic generative classifiers.

This section develops linear discriminant functions from binary hyperplanes and signed distances to unified multiclass classifiers with convex, singly connected decision regions. It presents least-squares classification and its matrix solution, constraints, non-probabilistic outputs, sensitivity to outliers, and weaknesses for multiclass data; develops Fisher’s discriminant, its covariance-based projection, thresholding and Gaussian interpretation, its equivalence to specially coded least squares, and its multiclass eigenvector generalization limited to K−1 features. It concludes with the perceptron algorithm, including its loss, updates, convergence behavior, history, implementation, and limitations, before introducing adaline and probabilistic generative classifiers.

nodes.title: 4.2. Probabilistic Generative Models
4.2.1 Continuous inputs
nodes.summary: The text develops probabilistic classification with logistic and softmax posteriors, then specializes to Gaussian class-conditional models. Shared covariance matrices cancel quadratic terms, yielding logistic or softmax generalized linear models with linear decision boundaries, while class priors shift boundaries through bias terms. Unequal covariances produce quadratic discriminants. It concludes by setting up maximum-likelihood estimation for a labeled two-class Gaussian model with shared covariance, binary targets, class prior pi, and the corresponding likelihood and log-likelihood.

nodes.title: 4.2.2 Maximum likelihood solution
nodes.summary: The text illustrates how Gaussian class covariances determine linear or quadratic classification boundaries, then derives maximum-likelihood estimates for priors, class means, and a shared pooled covariance in binary Gaussian classification, noting the extension to multiple classes and the lack of robustness to outliers. It next introduces naive Bayes for binary discrete features to avoid the exponentially large parameterization of unrestricted distributions, showing that the resulting class scores are linear and generalize to multicategory features, before beginning a discussion of exponential-family models.

nodes.title: 4.2.3 Discrete features
nodes.summary: The text derives the pooled maximum-likelihood covariance for Gaussian class models with shared covariance, notes its extension to multiple classes and its lack of robustness to outliers, and then develops naive Bayes classification for binary discrete features. It contrasts the exponentially large unrestricted probability table with the conditionally independent Bernoulli representation, derives linear log class scores and the equivalent binary logistic formulation, and notes the extension to multistate discrete variables before introducing the exponential-family perspective.

nodes.title: 4.2.4 Exponential family
nodes.summary: The text completes the shared-covariance Gaussian classification result, identifying the maximum-likelihood covariance as a class-size-weighted average of within-class covariances and noting its lack of robustness to outliers. It then develops classification with discrete features, explaining the exponential parameter growth of unrestricted models and the simplifying naive Bayes conditional-independence assumption, which yields linear discriminants and logistic classification. These Gaussian and discrete cases are unified through exponential-family class-conditional distributions with a shared scale, producing linear logits or softmax scores. Finally, it introduces probabilistic discriminative models, which estimate logistic or softmax parameters directly by maximum likelihood, with IRLS providing an efficient solution method.

This section develops probabilistic generative classification from Bayes' theorem, beginning with logistic posterior probabilities, the sigmoid, and log odds. It derives Gaussian classifiers for continuous inputs, showing how shared covariances yield linear logistic or softmax decision functions, unequal covariances yield quadratic boundaries, and maximum likelihood estimates priors, means, and pooled covariance while remaining sensitive to outliers. It then presents naive Bayes for discrete features, using conditional independence to avoid exponential parameter growth and obtain linear discriminants, and unifies the Gaussian and discrete cases through exponential-family models. Finally, it introduces discriminative logistic and softmax models trained directly by maximum likelihood, with IRLS as an efficient solution method.

nodes.title: 4.3. Probabilistic Discriminative Models
4.3.1 Fixed basis functions
nodes.summary: The text contrasts generative and discriminative classification, then introduces fixed nonlinear basis functions, which produce linear boundaries in feature space and nonlinear boundaries in the original input space. It discusses class overlap, posterior modeling, the role of a bias basis function, and the limitations of fixed transformations. It then defines two-class logistic regression as a sigmoid applied to a linear feature function, compares its linear parameter growth with the quadratic parameter growth of Gaussian generative models, and notes that maximum-likelihood estimation relies on the sigmoid derivative.

nodes.title: 4.3.2 Logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text introduces fixed nonlinear basis-function models, explaining their bias term, their inability to remove class overlap, their possible benefits for posterior modeling, and their limitations compared with adaptive basis functions. It then develops two-class logistic regression, in which class posteriors are modeled by a sigmoid of a linear feature function. Logistic regression requires far fewer parameters than a Gaussian generative model as feature dimension grows. For binary data, maximum likelihood leads to a Bernoulli likelihood and cross-entropy error, whose gradient is the prediction error times the feature vector, enabling sequential updates and mirroring linear regression. Finally, it explains the severe overfitting and non-finite maximum-likelihood solution caused by linearly separable data, including the continuum of equivalent separating hyperplanes, and notes that priors or regularization provide a remedy.

nodes.title: 4.3.3 Iterative reweighted least squares
IRLS
nodes.summary: The text derives the Newton update for logistic regression using the parameter-dependent diagonal matrix R with entries y_n(1 − y_n). The positive-definite Hessian ensures a unique optimum, and rewriting the update with the vector z reveals weighted least-squares normal equations. Because the weights change with w, the procedure is applied iteratively as IRLS. The weights represent the Bernoulli target variances, and the algorithm is also interpretable as solving a locally linearized problem in activation space, where z provides effective target values.

nodes.title: E[t] var[t]
nodes.summary: The text derives the Newton update for logistic regression, showing that its parameter-dependent positive-definite Hessian leads to a unique minimum and an iterative reweighted least-squares algorithm. It interprets the weights as Bernoulli variances and the adjusted response as an effective target from a local sigmoid linearization. It then introduces multiclass logistic regression using softmax probabilities and linear activations, derives the softmax derivatives, formulates the 1-of-K likelihood and cross-entropy error, and gives the gradient with respect to each class-specific parameter vector.

This section develops Newton–Raphson optimization for logistic regression, contrasts it with the one-step least-squares solution for linear regression, and derives the logistic gradient and positive-definite Hessian. Recasting the Newton step as weighted least squares produces the iterative reweighted least-squares algorithm, whose changing weights are Bernoulli variances and whose adjusted responses arise from a local sigmoid linearization. The section then generalizes the model to multiclass classification with softmax outputs, deriving the relevant derivatives, likelihood, cross-entropy error, and parameter gradients.

nodes.title: 4.3.4 Multiclass logistic regression
nodes.summary: The text develops multiclass logistic regression using softmax class probabilities, directly estimated weight vectors, and 1-of-K maximum-likelihood training. It derives the softmax Jacobian, multiclass likelihood, cross-entropy error, error-times-feature gradient, and block Hessian, noting the resulting sequential and Newton/IRLS algorithms, positive definiteness, and unique minimum. It then introduces probit regression as an alternative binary discriminative model motivated by thresholding a linear activation at a fixed threshold.

nodes.title: 4.3.5 Probit regression
nodes.summary: The text completes the multiclass logistic-regression discussion by deriving its error-times-feature gradient, Newton–Raphson/IRLS Hessian structure, and unique minimum. It then introduces probit regression through a stochastic threshold model, deriving the cumulative-distribution activation, Gaussian probit function, its relation to erf, maximum-likelihood estimation, and similarity to logistic regression. It compares logistic and probit sensitivity to outliers, explains a probabilistic treatment of label noise, and begins the treatment of canonical link functions by showing that exponential-family target distributions produce the common error-times-feature gradient and by deriving the conditional mean from the log normalizer.

nodes.title: 4.3.6 Canonical link functions
nodes.summary: The passage discusses classifier outliers and label noise, emphasizing the greater outlier sensitivity of probit regression and giving a probabilistic label-flip model. It then develops canonical link functions for generalized linear models, showing that exponential-family targets combined with the canonical activation produce a simple error-times-feature gradient, with Gaussian and logistic scale parameters as examples. Finally, it introduces the Laplace approximation as a tool needed for the more difficult Bayesian treatment of logistic regression.

This section develops probabilistic discriminative classification from the exponential-family basis, showing why shared-scale class-conditionals produce logistic and softmax posteriors that are linear in the input. It contrasts generative and direct discriminative training, introduces fixed-basis logistic regression, and covers likelihoods, cross-entropy, gradients, parameter efficiency, separability, overfitting, and regularization. It derives Newton optimization and IRLS for binary and multiclass models, including softmax derivatives and Hessian structure. The section also presents probit regression, compares its behavior with logistic regression under outliers and label noise, develops canonical link functions for exponential-family generalized linear models, and introduces the Laplace approximation for Bayesian logistic regression.

nodes.title: 4.4. The Laplace Approximation
4.4.1 Model comparison and BIC
nodes.summary: The text explains the strengths and limitations of the Laplace approximation, including its local Gaussian nature, usefulness for large datasets, handling of multimodal or constrained variables, and inability to capture global distributional structure. It derives how the approximation estimates normalization constants and Bayesian model evidence, introducing the Occam factor and the approximate BIC complexity penalty, contrasting BIC with AIC and noting problems caused by rank-deficient Hessians. It then begins Bayesian logistic regression, explaining why exact posterior and predictive inference is intractable and motivating a Laplace approximation based on a Gaussian prior, posterior mode, and Hessian.

The section first derives generalized-linear-model likelihood gradients and their simplification under the canonical link. It then develops the Laplace approximation by locally expanding the log density around a mode, producing a Gaussian whose precision is the negative second derivative or Hessian and requiring a genuine local maximum. The multivariate form, normalization, numerical mode-finding, and an illustrative example are presented. The approximation is subsequently used to estimate normalization constants and Bayesian model evidence, explaining the Occam factor, BIC’s complexity penalty, its contrast with AIC, and rank-deficient-Hessian limitations, before introducing its application to Bayesian logistic regression with a Gaussian prior.

nodes.title: 4.5. Bayesian Logistic Regression
4.5.1 Laplace approximation
nodes.summary: The text explains the Laplace approximation to Bayesian model evidence, including the Hessian at the posterior mode, Occam-factor complexity penalties, and the resulting approximate BIC criterion, while warning about rank-deficient Hessians and the limitations of AIC/BIC. It then introduces Bayesian logistic regression, whose exact posterior and predictive distributions are intractable, and develops a Laplace approximation using a Gaussian prior, MAP weights, and a Hessian-derived covariance. Finally, it formulates the predictive class probability as a posterior average of the logistic sigmoid and reduces the integral to the one-dimensional distribution of the weight projection onto the new feature vector.

nodes.title: 4.5.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops Bayesian logistic regression using a Gaussian posterior approximation centered at the MAP solution, with covariance determined by the Hessian. It reduces predictive marginalization over weights to a Gaussian integral over the scalar projection a = w^T phi, derives its mean and variance, and approximates the otherwise intractable sigmoid-Gaussian convolution through a rescaled probit function, yielding an explicit approximate predictive probability. The resulting decision boundary is unchanged from the MAP classifier for equal-prior misclassification, though uncertainty matters for other decision rules. The section also lists exercises on convex-hull characterization of linear separability and preservation of linear target constraints by least-squares predictions.

This section develops Laplace-approximated Bayesian logistic regression, beginning with its use for model evidence, Hessian-based Occam penalties, and approximate BIC, together with relevant caveats. It then constructs a Gaussian approximation around the logistic-regression MAP solution and derives predictive probabilities by reducing weight marginalization to a one-dimensional Gaussian projection and approximating the sigmoid integral with a rescaled probit. It discusses the implications for decision boundaries and presents exercises on linear separability and least-squares constraints.

nodes.title: 4.1 ( ) Given a set of data points {x n }, we can define the convex hull to be the set of all points x given by
nodes.summary: The text derives a Gaussian-convolution approximation for the logistic sigmoid, defines the scaling factor κ, and applies it to obtain an approximate predictive distribution for logistic classification. It explains that posterior marginalization leaves the equal-prior misclassification decision boundary unchanged but can affect other decision criteria, and refers to a variational-inference illustration. It then presents exercises on the relationship between convex-hull intersection and linear separability, and on preservation of linear constraints by least-squares predictions.

nodes.title: 4.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text completes the Gaussian marginalization of a logistic sigmoid by introducing a variance-dependent scaling factor, derives the approximate predictive probability, and explains why marginalization leaves the equal-prior 0.5 decision boundary unchanged while potentially affecting other decisions. It then presents Exercises 4.1–4.10 covering convex-hull separability, preservation of linear target constraints by least-squares models, extensions to multiple constraints, class-separation and Fisher criteria, covariance-based least-squares classification, logistic-sigmoid identities, Gaussian generative posterior derivation, and maximum-likelihood estimates for class priors and class means.

nodes.title: 4.4 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on constrained least-squares linear models, class separation and Fisher criteria, covariance-based least-squares classification, logistic sigmoid properties, posterior probabilities and parameters in two-class Gaussian generative models, and maximum-likelihood estimation of class priors and class means in multiclass generative models with 1-of-K targets and shared-covariance Gaussian densities.

nodes.title: 4.7 ( ) www
nodes.summary: This exercise section covers linear-model bias terms and preservation of linear target constraints, derivation of the optimal class-separation direction and equivalent forms of the Fisher criterion, the relationship between least-squares classification and covariance matrices, key identities and inversion of the logistic sigmoid, derivation of posterior probabilities and parameters for two-class Gaussian generative models, and maximum-likelihood estimates of class priors and class means in multiclass generative models with 1-of-K targets and shared-covariance Gaussian densities.

nodes.title: 4.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: This section presents exercises on linear models for classification, covering bias terms, preservation of linear constraints by least-squares models, class-separation and Fisher criteria, covariance-based least-squares solutions, logistic sigmoid identities and derivatives, Gaussian generative classification, maximum-likelihood estimation of class priors, means, and shared covariances, naive Bayes with discrete features, logistic-regression gradients and optimization properties, behavior on linearly separable data, and likelihood formulation for probabilistically mislabelled binary targets.

nodes.title: 4.12 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text states the maximum-likelihood estimates for class means and a shared covariance as a class-prior-weighted average of within-class covariances. It then presents exercises covering the linearity of softmax arguments in a discrete naive Bayes model, verification of the logistic-sigmoid derivative and logistic-regression gradient, behavior of maximum likelihood for linearly separable data, positive definiteness of the logistic-regression Hessian and uniqueness of its minimum, and formulation of the log likelihood when class labels are probabilistic rather than exact.

nodes.title: 4.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text states the maximum-likelihood estimates for class means and the shared covariance as a prior-weighted average of within-class covariances, then presents exercises on naive Bayes with discrete independent features, derivatives of the logistic sigmoid and logistic-regression error, behavior under linearly separable data, positive definiteness and uniqueness properties of the logistic-regression Hessian and error function, and likelihood construction for probabilistically mislabeled binary training data.

nodes.title: 4.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 4.17–4.25 cover derivatives and gradients for softmax and cross-entropy models; gradient and Hessian derivation for probit regression and its use in IRLS; positive semidefiniteness of the multiclass logistic-regression Hessian; the relationship between the probit and error functions; derivation of Laplace-approximated model evidence and the BIC approximation under a broad Gaussian prior and i.i.d. data; Gaussian marginalization of logistic regression; and matching logistic and scaled-probit sigmoid derivatives at zero to obtain λ² = π/8.

nodes.title: 4.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on deriving softmax derivatives and cross-entropy gradients; obtaining probit-regression likelihood gradients and Hessians for IRLS; proving positive semidefiniteness of the multiclass logistic-regression Hessian; relating probit and erf functions; deriving Laplace-approximation model evidence and the BIC; marginalizing logistic regression under a Gaussian parameter posterior; matching logistic and scaled-probit sigmoid derivatives; and proving a Gaussian-convolution identity for the probit function.

This section presents linear models for classification, beginning with binary and multiclass decision boundaries, target encodings, discriminant functions, generalized linear models, least-squares classification, Fisher discriminants, and perceptrons. It then develops probabilistic generative methods including logistic posteriors, Gaussian classifiers, naive Bayes, and exponential-family models, followed by discriminative logistic, softmax, and probit regression with likelihood-based training, regularization, Newton methods, and IRLS. The section derives and applies the Laplace approximation to model evidence and Bayesian logistic regression, including Occam penalties, BIC, posterior and predictive approximations, and sigmoid marginalization. Exercises reinforce linear separability, covariance and Fisher analyses, constrained least squares, sigmoid and softmax calculus, Gaussian and naive-Bayes classification, optimization and Hessian properties, separable and noisy labels, probit models, Bayesian evidence, and logistic–probit approximations.

nodes.title: 5 Neural Networks
5.1. Feed-forward Network Functions
5.1.1 Weight-space symmetries
nodes.summary: The text demonstrates feed-forward networks’ ability to approximate several nonlinear functions and solve a synthetic classification problem, highlighting how hidden units combine to form the final mapping and noting that both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian methods provide effective solutions. It then explains weight-space symmetries: sign flips and hidden-unit permutations create multiple equivalent parameter settings, yielding an M!2^M symmetry factor for two-layer networks and corresponding products across deeper layers. These symmetries generally apply beyond tanh networks, are usually of limited practical consequence, but matter for Bayesian model comparison. Finally, it introduces network training as parameter estimation for nonlinear input-output mappings using a sum-of-squares objective over training data.

This section introduces feed-forward neural networks as adaptive nonlinear extensions of linear models. It develops their layered computation of weighted inputs, biases, hidden activations, and task-dependent outputs, explains forward propagation and the MLP interpretation, and discusses bias absorption, differentiability, linear versus nonlinear hidden units, deeper and skip-connected architectures, and layer-count terminology. It also covers nonlinear function approximation and classification, effective maximum-likelihood and Bayesian training, equivalent parameter settings caused by hidden-unit sign and permutation symmetries, their relevance to Bayesian comparison, and parameter estimation using training objectives such as summed squared error.

nodes.title: 5.2. Network Training
5.2.1 Parameter optimization
nodes.summary: The text introduces softmax outputs and their corresponding multiclass cross-entropy loss, explains softmax invariance and regularization, and summarizes the appropriate activation/error pairs for regression and classification. It then describes neural-network training as minimizing a nonlinear error surface, using gradients and stationary-point analysis to distinguish minima, maxima, and saddle points. It discusses equivalent solutions from hidden-unit symmetries, local versus global minima, and the practical use of iterative numerical optimization. Finally, it motivates gradient-based methods through a local Taylor expansion that approximates the error function quadratically around a chosen weight vector.

nodes.title: 5.2.2 Local quadratic approximation
nodes.summary: The text explains neural-network error optimization: stationary points, equivalent and inequivalent minima, and the distinction between global and local minima; it then motivates iterative numerical optimization. It develops a local quadratic Taylor model using the gradient and Hessian, analyzes minima through Hessian eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and shows that positive definiteness produces elliptical error contours. Finally, it introduces the efficiency benefits of gradient information, obtainable through backpropagation, noting that a quadratic model over W parameters contains O(W²) relevant information.

nodes.title: 5.2.3 Use of gradient information
nodes.summary: The text explains how the Hessian characterizes quadratic error surfaces and minima: eigenvector coordinates produce elliptical contours, and positive eigenvalues are necessary and sufficient for positive definiteness and a local minimum. It then shows why efficiently computed gradients make neural-network training computationally feasible, contrasting O(W^3) derivative-free optimization with O(W^2) gradient-based optimization. It presents batch gradient descent and its learning-rate update, notes its inefficiency relative to conjugate-gradient and quasi-Newton methods, discusses repeated random initializations and validation, and introduces online or stochastic gradient descent, which updates weights using individual data points from a summed maximum-likelihood error.

nodes.title: 5.2.4 Gradient descent optimization
nodes.summary: The text explains why gradient information and error backpropagation make neural-network optimization computationally practical. It presents batch gradient descent, its learning-rate update rule and limitations, more efficient conjugate-gradient and quasi-Newton alternatives, repeated random restarts with validation, and online or stochastic gradient descent, including its advantages for redundant data and escaping local minima. It then introduces backpropagation as an efficient forward-and-backward method for computing weight derivatives, emphasizing that derivative evaluation and weight updating are separate stages and that backpropagation is not limited to multilayer perceptrons, gradient descent, or sum-of-squares error.

This section develops neural-network training from probabilistic error modeling to practical optimization. It derives regression training from a Gaussian likelihood, including maximum-likelihood weights and noise precision, then extends the activation/error-function pairing to binary and multiclass classification through sigmoid and softmax outputs with cross-entropy losses. It explains the nonconvex, symmetry-rich error landscape and distinguishes local and global minima, maxima, and saddle points. Local quadratic Taylor models and Hessian eigenanalysis motivate gradient-based optimization, including batch, conjugate-gradient, quasi-Newton, and stochastic methods, with repeated initialization and validation. Finally, it explains how backpropagation makes gradient computation efficient and separates derivative evaluation from the subsequent weight-update algorithm.

nodes.title: 5.3. Error Backpropagation
5.3.1 Evaluation of error-function derivatives
Error Backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text derives hidden-unit error signals for neural-network backpropagation using the chain rule, yielding δj = h′(aj) ∑k wkjδk, and explains how these signals are recursively propagated backward through arbitrary feed-forward topologies. It presents the complete backpropagation procedure, batch-gradient calculation, and extension to unit-specific activation functions. It then introduces a two-layer illustrative network with tanh hidden units, linear outputs, and sum-of-squares error, defining the tanh function, its derivative, the error function, and the associated forward-propagation equations.

This section develops backpropagation for general feed-forward neural networks. It begins with per-pattern error gradients and a linear sum-of-squares example, then introduces weighted inputs, nonlinear activations, bias units, and forward propagation. Using the chain rule, it defines local error signals and shows that each weight gradient is the product of the downstream error signal and the upstream activation; output and recursively propagated hidden-unit signals provide the full algorithm for sequential or batch training. The treatment also covers arbitrary differentiable and unit-specific activations and illustrates the results with a tanh-hidden, linear-output network using sum-of-squares error, while noting broader derivative and optimization methods.

nodes.title: 5.3.2 A simple example
nodes.summary: The text explains that batch backpropagation sums per-pattern gradients and can accommodate unit-specific activation functions. It then works through a two-layer tanh-hidden, linear-output network with sum-of-squares error, giving the forward-pass equations, output and hidden error signals, and gradients for both layers. Finally, it discusses backpropagation's O(W) computational efficiency and contrasts it with forward and central finite-difference derivative estimates, including their truncation errors, roundoff limitations, doubled cost for central differences, and loss of O(W) scaling.

nodes.title: 5.3.3 Efficiency of backpropagation
nodes.summary: The text gives the backpropagation formulas for output and hidden-unit errors and for derivatives of weights, then explains its O(W) efficiency compared with finite-difference methods, whose O(W²) cost makes them unsuitable for training despite their usefulness for implementation checks. It introduces the Jacobian of network outputs with respect to inputs and shows how Jacobians enable chain-rule error propagation through differentiable modules in modular systems.

nodes.title: 5.3.4 The Jacobian matrix
nodes.summary: The text explains numerical differentiation as a costly but useful implementation check, then develops Jacobian computation by backpropagation for network outputs with respect to inputs. It describes the Jacobian’s use in modular systems and local propagation of input errors, gives recursive formulas and sigmoid or softmax output conditions, and outlines forward and numerical-difference methods for verification. It then introduces the Hessian of the network error, explains its construction from weight and bias parameters, lists its roles in optimization, retraining, pruning, and Bayesian inference, and notes that it can be calculated exactly through an extension of backpropagation.

This section presents error backpropagation as an efficient chain-rule method for computing gradients in feed-forward neural networks, clearly separating derivative evaluation from optimization updates and relating batch, online, and minibatch training. It develops forward and backward propagation for general activations, biases, output and hidden error signals, and weight gradients, including a detailed tanh-hidden, linear-output example. It explains the method's O(W) efficiency and contrasts it with finite differences, then extends the ideas to Jacobians for input-output sensitivity and modular systems, and to exact Hessian computation for optimization, pruning, retraining, and Bayesian inference.

nodes.title: 5.4. The Hessian Matrix
5.4.1 Diagonal approximation
nodes.summary: This section discusses efficient approximations to neural-network Hessians. It derives a diagonal approximation with O(W) evaluation by recursively backpropagating only diagonal second derivatives, contrasts it with exact diagonal computation and the O(W^2) full Hessian, and warns that strongly nondiagonal Hessians limit its accuracy. For sum-of-squares regression, it derives the Levenberg–Marquardt or outer-product approximation by dropping a residual-weighted second-derivative term, explains when that omission is justified, gives its computational cost and formula, and presents the corresponding weighted formula for logistic cross-entropy and the analogous softmax result.

nodes.title: 5.4.2 Outer product approximation
nodes.summary: The text derives the Hessian for a neural network using sum-of-squares regression error and explains when its residual-weighted second-derivative component can be ignored, leading to the Levenberg–Marquardt or outer product approximation based on first derivatives. It describes the computational cost, cautions that the approximation depends on suitable training, and gives analogous forms for logistic-sigmoid cross-entropy and softmax multiclass networks, while also listing related exercises.

nodes.title: 5.4.3 Inverse Hessian
nodes.summary: The text presents a sequential rank-one outer-product approximation for efficiently computing an inverse Hessian, derives its update using the Sherman–Morrison/Woodbury identity, explains regularized initialization, dataset processing, multi-output extension, and the relation to quasi-Newton methods. It then describes estimating Hessian elements by four-point finite differences, noting truncation and numerical-precision limitations.

nodes.title: 5.4.4 Finite differences
nodes.summary: The text presents three approaches to Hessian computation in neural networks. An outer-product approximation enables sequential inverse-Hessian updates via the Woodbury identity, starting from a small diagonal regularizer and processing the data in one pass; this extends to multiple outputs and relates to quasi-Newton methods. Finite-difference evaluation can use direct error differences at O(W^3) cost or gradient differences obtained by backpropagation at O(W^2) cost, with central differences providing second-order accuracy. Finally, exact Hessians can be computed by extending backpropagation to arbitrary differentiable feed-forward networks in O(W^2) time; for a two-layer network, the derivation begins by defining output-error derivatives and specifying the Hessian block for pairs of second-layer weights.

nodes.title: 5.4.5 Exact evaluation of the Hessian
nodes.summary: The text compares numerical, exact, and Hessian-vector methods for neural-network Hessian computation. Direct symmetric finite differences achieve O(δ²) accuracy but cost O(W³), while finite differences of backpropagated gradients cost O(W²). An exact backpropagation-based Hessian evaluation works for arbitrary differentiable feed-forward networks and error functions, scales as O(W²), and is given for a two-layer network through three weight-block formulas, with provisions for biases and skip connections. Finally, it explains that Hessian-vector products can be computed directly in O(W) time and storage by applying the differential operator R = vᵀ∇ to the ordinary forward- and backpropagation equations.

nodes.title: 5.4.6 Fast multiplication by the Hessian
nodes.summary: The text completes formulas for Hessian elements in a two-layer network, including treatment of biases and skip connections, then presents Pearlmutter/Møller fast Hessian-vector multiplication using the differential operator R{·} applied to forward propagation, backpropagation, and gradient equations. The method computes v^T H in linear time and storage, is easy to implement, and can reconstruct the full Hessian with repeated unit-vector products. It then begins neural-network regularization, discussing how the hidden-unit count M controls model complexity, how local minima and initialization affect validation performance, selection of M using validation error, and the use of quadratic regularization to prevent overfitting.

This section introduces the Hessian of a neural-network error function and its applications in optimization, retraining, pruning, and Bayesian inference. It develops diagonal and outer-product approximations, including regression, logistic, and softmax forms; derives efficient inverse-Hessian updates and relates them to quasi-Newton methods; compares finite-difference approaches with their accuracy and computational costs; and presents exact backpropagation-based Hessian evaluation, including biases and skip connections. It concludes with linear-time Hessian-vector products and begins applying these ideas to model complexity and regularization.

nodes.title: 5.5. Regularization in Neural Networks
5.5.1 Consistent Gaussian priors
nodes.summary: The text discusses neural-network regularization through L2 weight decay, its Gaussian-prior interpretation, and its limitations under affine rescaling of inputs and outputs. It develops transformation-consistent layer-specific Gaussian priors, explains the issue of unconstrained biases and the use of separate bias hyperparameters, and generalizes the approach to grouped priors leading to automatic relevance determination. It also introduces early stopping as an alternative complexity-control method based on monitoring validation error, which initially falls and later rises as overfitting develops. The accompanying figures illustrate network fits of different sizes and the effects of local minima and random initialization.

nodes.title: 5.5.2 Early stopping
nodes.summary: The text discusses structured weight priors and regularization, noting their transformation properties, the problems caused by improper priors with unconstrained biases, the use of separate bias hyperparameters, grouped weight priors, and automatic relevance determination. It explains early stopping as a complexity-control method: training error decreases while validation error eventually increases through overfitting, so training is stopped at minimum validation error. Early stopping is interpreted as limiting growing effective degrees of freedom and, for quadratic errors, is quantitatively related to weight decay through the iteration-count/learning-rate product. The text then introduces invariance requirements in pattern recognition, explains why learning invariances solely from transformed training examples can be impractical, and begins describing four alternative approaches, starting with data augmentation.

nodes.title: 5.5.3 Invariances
nodes.summary: The text discusses early stopping as a generalization method and explains its similarity to weight decay, then introduces input-transformation invariances in neural networks. It presents four ways to enforce invariance—data augmentation, regularization via tangent propagation, invariant preprocessing features, and invariant network or kernel architectures—along with their benefits and limitations. It also illustrates synthetic image warping and begins the geometric formulation of tangent propagation, in which continuous transformations trace manifolds and are locally represented by tangent vectors.

nodes.title: 5.5.4 Tangent propagation
nodes.summary: The text discusses transformation-based regularization for neural networks. It presents synthetic digit warping and notes that invariant hand-crafted features may either extrapolate well or lose discriminative information. Tangent propagation enforces local invariance by penalizing the network’s output derivatives along tangent directions generated by continuous input transformations; it defines the transformation manifold, tangent vectors, Jacobian-based output derivatives, regularized objective, finite-difference implementation, multi-parameter extensions, and implications for combined transformations. It also introduces tangent distance for nearest-neighbour methods and begins explaining the close relationship between invariance through transformed training data and tangent propagation using an infinite-data sum-of-squares formulation.

nodes.title: 5.5.5 Training with transformed data
nodes.summary: The text explains tangent distance and how training on transformed data produces tangent-propagation regularization. A Taylor expansion of small, zero-mean input transformations shows that the augmented-data loss equals the original loss plus a variance-weighted penalty on sensitivity along transformation directions; for additive noise this becomes Tikhonov regularization, which penalizes the input-gradient norm and can be optimized by extended backpropagation. It then introduces convolutional neural networks as an architectural way to encode invariance to translations, scaling, rotations, and elastic deformations in handwritten-digit recognition, while exploiting the local correlations of nearby pixels through local feature extraction and hierarchical combination.

nodes.title: 5.5.6 Convolutional networks
nodes.summary: The text explains how small input perturbations simplify regularization into a gradient penalty, with additive noise yielding Tikhonov regularization, and notes its connection to noise-based generalization and extended backpropagation. It then introduces convolutional neural networks as a structural means of achieving image-transformation invariance, describing local receptive fields, shared weights, feature maps, convolution, subsampling, stacked layers, training, and parameter reduction. Finally, it introduces soft weight sharing, which replaces exact equality constraints with learned regularization that groups weights around learned means with learned spreads.

nodes.title: 5.5.7 Soft weight sharing
nodes.summary: The text describes convolutional and subsampling network architecture, including feature maps, local receptive fields, shift invariance, progressive convolution/subsampling stages, softmax output, backpropagation with shared weights, and parameter reduction. It then presents soft weight sharing as a Gaussian-mixture regularizer: weights are encouraged to cluster around learned means, with learned variances and mixing coefficients, and the resulting objective and derivatives are given for weights, means, variances, and softmax-parameterized mixing coefficients. Finally, it introduces Mixture Density Networks for modeling multimodal conditional distributions, motivating them with inverse kinematics, other ambiguous inverse problems, and a toy multimodal dataset.

This section examines regularization and complexity control in neural networks. It covers model-size selection, L2 weight decay and its Gaussian-prior interpretation, transformation-consistent and grouped priors including automatic relevance determination, and early stopping. It then addresses invariance to input transformations through data augmentation, tangent propagation, invariant features, and specialized architectures, deriving tangent-propagation and noise-induced Tikhonov penalties and relating them to transformed-data training. Convolutional networks are presented as an architectural approach to image invariance and efficient parameter sharing, followed by soft weight sharing through learned Gaussian-mixture priors and an introduction to Mixture Density Networks for multimodal conditional modeling.

nodes.title: 5.6. Mixture Density Networks
nodes.summary: The text introduces mixture density networks as a solution to inverse and other multimodal prediction problems that ordinary Gaussian, least-squares regression handles poorly. Using robot-arm kinematics and a toy sinusoidal inverse problem, it motivates modeling p(t|x) with input-dependent Gaussian mixtures whose coefficients, means, and variances are produced by a neural network. It explains the output parameterization, likelihood training, posterior-responsibility-based backpropagation derivatives, and how the model represents changing unimodal or multimodal densities. It also gives formulas and interpretations for the conditional mean and variance, discusses the limitations of means for multimodal outputs and the use of conditional modes, and briefly begins Bayesian neural networks by contrasting maximum-likelihood/MAP estimation with parameter marginalization and noting the need for variational approximations because exact inference is intractable.

nodes.title: 5.7. Bayesian Neural Networks
5.7.1 Posterior parameter distribution
nodes.summary: This section develops Bayesian neural-network regression using a Laplace approximation to the weight posterior and a local linearization of the network around its MAP parameters. It specifies Gaussian likelihood and weight-prior models, derives the approximate posterior from the Hessian, and obtains a Gaussian predictive distribution whose variance combines observation noise with parameter uncertainty. It then applies the evidence framework to estimate alpha and beta and compare network models, deriving the approximate log evidence and beginning the eigenvalue-based update for alpha.

nodes.title: 5.7.2 Hyperparameter optimization
nodes.summary: The text completes Bayesian neural-network regression by describing the Gaussian predictive distribution, whose mean is the MAP network output and whose variance combines observation noise with input-dependent parameter uncertainty. It then develops evidence-based optimization of the prior and noise hyperparameters alpha and beta using a Laplace approximation, giving the approximate log evidence, regularized MAP error, Hessian-eigenvalue expression for the effective parameter count, and iterative re-estimation formulas. It discusses complications from neural-network multimodality, initialization dependence, equivalent hidden-unit symmetries, inequivalent solutions, evidence-based comparison of architectures, marginalization over hyperparameters, and the numerical difficulty of evaluating Hessian determinants. Symmetry multiplicities may be included in the evidence, and Bayesian neural-network classification is introduced as the following section.

nodes.title: 5.7.3 Bayesian neural networks for classification
nodes.summary: The text completes the evidence-based Laplace treatment of Bayesian neural-network regression, defining the effective parameter count and β re-estimation, explaining alternating hyperparameter/posterior optimization, multimodal and symmetry-equivalent solutions, evidence-based model comparison, and the practical difficulty of Hessian determinants. It then develops Bayesian neural-network classification with a logistic output: binary cross-entropy likelihood, Gaussian prior and α regularization, MAP training, Hessian and Laplace posterior approximation, evidence optimization, and predictive probabilities. A point-estimate prediction is contrasted with an uncertainty-aware approximation obtained by linearizing the output preactivation, yielding a Gaussian activation distribution and an approximate sigmoid-Gaussian integral; examples show reduced overfitting and less confident predictions. The text ends with exercises on converting sigmoid hidden units to tanh units and relating multioutput likelihood maximization to sum-of-squares minimization.

This section introduces Bayesian neural networks as a probabilistic extension of maximum-likelihood and MAP-trained networks. It develops Laplace-approximated posterior and predictive distributions for regression, including uncertainty from both observation noise and parameter uncertainty, and uses Bayesian evidence to optimize hyperparameters and compare models. It discusses practical difficulties caused by nonconvex multimodal posteriors, parameter symmetries, initialization, and Hessian computations. It then extends the treatment to logistic classification, deriving MAP and Laplace methods and uncertainty-aware predictive probabilities through a linearized sigmoid model, with examples demonstrating reduced overfitting and confidence. The section concludes with related exercises.

nodes.title: 6 Kernel Methods
6.1. Dual Representations
nodes.summary: The text derives the dual form of regularized linear least-squares regression. The optimal weight vector is represented as a linear combination of training feature vectors, allowing the problem to be rewritten using the Gram matrix of kernel evaluations. The dual coefficients are a = (K + λI)^{-1}t, and predictions are kernel-weighted combinations of training targets. Although the dual formulation may involve a larger matrix inversion, it avoids explicit feature construction and permits implicitly working in high- or infinite-dimensional spaces. The text notes that this duality extends to other linear models and connects to Gaussian processes and support vector machines. It then introduces kernel construction, either through an explicit feature map or directly through valid inner-product functions, including a squared inner-product example.

nodes.title: 6.2. Constructing Kernels
nodes.summary: The text derives the dual kernel form of regularized linear regression, showing that predictions are weighted combinations of training targets based solely on kernel evaluations. Although the dual form involves an N×N matrix, its key benefit is implicit access to high- or infinite-dimensional feature spaces and its broader relevance to models such as perceptrons, Gaussian processes, and support vector machines. It then explains how kernels arise from feature mappings or can be constructed directly, with validity characterized by positive-semidefinite Gram matrices. It presents kernel-combination rules and examples including polynomial, Gaussian, generalized kernel-distance, and set kernels, and extends kernels to symbolic objects and generative-model constructions, including latent-variable, sequence/HMM, and Fisher kernels. The sigmoidal kernel is noted as a commonly used but generally invalid positive-semidefinite kernel. Finally, the text introduces radial basis function networks, exact interpolation with centers at training points, overfitting under noise, and regularized Green’s-function expansions.

nodes.title: 6.3. Radial Basis Function Networks
6.3.1 Nadaraya-Watson model
nodes.summary: The text explains how radial-basis-function centres may be selected randomly, by orthogonal least squares, or by clustering, then develops the Nadaraya-Watson kernel-regression model from Parzen estimation of the joint input-target density. Under a zero-mean component assumption, the conditional mean is a normalized, locality-weighted sum of training targets with weights satisfying a summation constraint. The method also yields a full conditional distribution; Gaussian components produce a Gaussian-mixture conditional model illustrated on sinusoidal data. Extensions include flexible Gaussian components and general Gaussian-mixture models, which can reduce prediction cost by using fewer components while increasing training cost. The section concludes by transitioning to Gaussian processes.

Radial basis function networks model functions as linear combinations of distance-based basis functions. The section covers their origins in exact interpolation, regularized solutions, and noisy-input modeling; explains normalized radial bases and the Nadaraya-Watson kernel-regression formulation; and discusses practical networks with fewer data-selected centres fitted by least squares. It further develops conditional-density and Gaussian-mixture interpretations, including flexible components and the trade-off between training and prediction cost, before introducing the connection to Gaussian processes.

nodes.title: 6.4. Gaussian Processes
6.4.1 Linear regression revisited
nodes.summary: The text introduces Gaussian processes as Bayesian priors over functions rather than parameterized regression weights, emphasizing that finite datasets reduce inference to finite jointly Gaussian function values. It derives a Gaussian process from linear regression with Gaussian weight priors, showing that the induced covariance is a kernel Gram matrix, then formally defines Gaussian processes through their finite-dimensional Gaussian distributions, usually with zero mean and covariance given by a kernel. Directly specified Gaussian and exponential kernels are presented, with connections to the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process and other established models. The text then develops Gaussian-process regression by adding independent Gaussian observation noise, specifying the latent-function and conditional target distributions, explaining the similarity interpretation of kernels, and showing that integrating out the latent function yields a Gaussian marginal distribution for the targets.

nodes.title: 6.4.2 Gaussian processes for regression
nodes.summary: The text develops Gaussian process regression with independent Gaussian observation noise, deriving the marginal target covariance by adding kernel and noise covariances and giving the Gaussian predictive mean and variance for new inputs. It presents a flexible quadratic-exponential kernel with constant and linear terms, explains positive-semidefinite kernel requirements, interprets predictions as kernel or radial-basis expansions, and compares Gaussian-process and finite-basis computational costs. Figures illustrate Gaussian-process samples, noisy data generation, conditional prediction, and uncertainty growth away from training data. The section also discusses large-data approximations and extensions such as co-kriging, manifold learning, and stochastic differential equations. Finally, it explains learning covariance hyperparameters through marginal-likelihood optimization and gradients, the effects of nonconvexity and priors, the difficulty of full Bayesian marginalization, and the need for input-dependent noise models in heteroscedastic regression.

nodes.title: 6.4.3 Learning the hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text discusses Gaussian process applications, hyperparameter learning through likelihood maximization and gradient optimization, the likelihood-gradient formulas, nonconvexity and Bayesian treatment of hyperparameters, and extensions for input-dependent noise. It then introduces automatic relevance determination, explaining how separate kernel precision parameters reveal and potentially remove irrelevant input variables, with a kernel example, prior-sample illustration, and a synthetic demonstration setup.

nodes.title: 6.4.4 Automatic relevance determination
nodes.summary: The text introduces input-dependent variance modeling with a GP for ln β(x), explains automatic relevance determination through separate input precisions optimized by marginal likelihood, and shows how small precisions reveal irrelevant or weakly informative variables. It presents illustrative prior samples, a synthetic three-input experiment, and an ARD-enhanced regression kernel. It then begins Gaussian-process classification, explaining that a latent real-valued GP is transformed by a logistic sigmoid to produce binary-class probabilities.

nodes.title: 6.4.5 Gaussian processes for classification
nodes.summary: The text first demonstrates ARD for Gaussian-process regression: marginal-likelihood optimization assigns large relevance to a strong predictor, smaller relevance to a noisy predictor, and near-zero relevance to an irrelevant input, and gives the corresponding ARD kernel. It then introduces Gaussian-process classification by passing a latent Gaussian-process function through a logistic sigmoid, yielding a Bernoulli likelihood for binary targets. The latent variables have a zero-mean Gaussian prior with a kernel covariance plus a small numerical diagonal term. Binary prediction requires integrating the sigmoid over the latent posterior, an analytically intractable calculation addressed by sampling or Gaussian approximations. Variational inference, expectation propagation, and Laplace approximation are identified as the main approaches; the text notes variational extensions to multiclass problems and begins deriving the Laplace method by factoring the predictive posterior through the training latent variables.

nodes.title: 6.4.6 Laplace approximation
nodes.summary: The text develops Gaussian-process classification, focusing on approximating the intractable logistic predictive integral. It reviews variational inference and expectation propagation, then derives the Laplace approximation in detail: the latent posterior's mode is found by Newton-Raphson/IRLS, its positive-definite Hessian establishes a unique mode, and a Gaussian approximation yields predictive means and variances. Laplace approximation is also applied to marginal-likelihood evaluation and covariance-parameter optimization, including derivatives accounting for posterior-mode dependence. A synthetic binary-class example and multiclass extension are noted. Finally, the text explains the infinite-hidden-unit connection between Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes, including the loss of output coupling and the nonstationary kernels induced by probit or Gaussian activations with zero-centered weight priors.

nodes.title: 6.4.7 Connection to neural networks

Weight marginalization is implicit in the kernel view, whereas hyperparameters determine function length scales and generally require numerical treatment. The section concludes with exercises on dual least-squares regression, dual perceptrons, kernelized nearest neighbours, matrix definiteness, valid-kernel constructions, and a function-matching kernel.

nodes.title: 7 Sparse Kernel Machines
7.1. Maximum Margin Classifiers
Joseph-Louis Lagrange
nodes.summary: The text derives the kernelized dual form of the maximum-margin classifier, explains its quadratic-programming constraints, computational implications, and the importance of positive-definite kernels, and gives the kernel prediction equation. A Gaussian-kernel example illustrates nonlinear separation and sparsity. The section then introduces overlapping class distributions and slack variables, which allow margin violations and misclassification through a linear penalty.

nodes.title: 7.1.1 Overlapping class distributions
nodes.summary: The text explains soft-margin and ν-support vector machines for overlapping class distributions. Slack variables permit margin violations and misclassification, while C balances margin maximization against training error. Lagrangian and KKT analysis yields the dual quadratic program with box constraints, identifies support-vector types, and provides the bias and prediction formulas. It introduces ν-SVM and interprets ν as bounds on margin errors and support-vector fractions. Because direct quadratic programming is costly, chunking, decomposition, and especially SMO are discussed. The text also explains why kernels do not remove the curse of dimensionality, illustrates an implicit polynomial feature space, and describes Platt sigmoid calibration for probabilistic SVM outputs, including its independence requirement and limitations. It concludes by beginning a comparison between soft-margin SVMs and regularized logistic regression.

nodes.title: 7.1.3 Multiclass SVMs

It then surveys multiclass SVM strategies: one-versus-the-rest and its target modification, joint multiclass optimization, one-versus-one voting, DAGSVM, and error-correcting output codes, including their ambiguities, class imbalance, robustness, and computational costs. It also introduces single-class SVMs for enclosing high-density regions, describing hyperplane- and sphere-based methods and their equivalence for translation-invariant kernels, before beginning the discussion of sparse SVM regression.

Finally, it introduces PAC learning, generalization error, confidence and error thresholds, training-size bounds, and VC dimension as a measure of hypothesis-space complexity.

nodes.title: 7.2. Relevance Vector Machines

nodes.summary: The text contrasts conservative PAC and PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds with the practical motivation for relevance vector machines. It introduces RVM regression as a Bayesian Gaussian linear model using arbitrary nonlinear or kernel basis functions and separate weight-precision hyperparameters. Evidence maximization yields Gaussian posterior weights and automatically prunes many parameters, leaving sparse relevance vectors. The text gives the marginal likelihood, posterior, hyperparameter re-estimation equations, predictive mean and variance, and notes an equivalent EM approach. It discusses overconfident extrapolation compared with Gaussian processes, illustrates RVM sparsity and comparable accuracy to SVMs, and outlines RVM disadvantages involving nonconvex optimization and computational cost, while noting that model complexity and noise are learned automatically. The section concludes by beginning a more detailed analysis of the sparsity mechanism.

nodes.title: 7.2.2 Analysis of sparsity

nodes.summary: The text explains how the relative quality and sparsity of a basis function determine the marginal-likelihood optimum for its hyperparameter: q_i^2 > s_i yields a finite update, while q_i^2 ≤ s_i leads to αi = ∞ and pruning. It presents the resulting sequential sparse Bayesian learning algorithm for adding, updating, and removing basis functions, defines computational forms for the quality and sparsity quantities, and notes that the cost depends on the typically small active set. It then introduces the extension of the RVM to binary classification using an ARD prior and a logistic-sigmoid linear model.

This section analyzes how automatic relevance determination produces RVM sparsity: basis functions poorly aligned with or weakly supported by the data reduce the marginal likelihood unless they are pruned. By isolating each basis function’s contribution to the marginal likelihood, it defines its sparsity and quality measures and derives explicit relevance conditions and updates. These results lead to a sequential sparse Bayesian learning algorithm that efficiently adds, updates, or removes basis functions, followed by an extension of the RVM framework to binary classification with an ARD prior and logistic-sigmoid model.
