nodes.title: 8 Graphical Models
8.1. Bayesian Networks
8.1.1 Example: Polynomial regression
nodes.summary: The text explains how directed acyclic graphs encode joint distributions through products of node-specific conditional distributions given their parents, illustrates the factorization with a seven-node graph, and describes the DAG restriction and normalization properties. It then applies graphical models to Bayesian polynomial regression, introducing plates for repeated observations, explicit deterministic parameters, notation for observed and latent variables, posterior inference for coefficients, and predictive inference for new inputs by integrating out the coefficients. Finally, it presents ancestral sampling, in which variables are sampled in topological order to generate joint or marginal samples from a DAG-defined distribution.

nodes.title: 8.1.2 Generative models
nodes.summary: The text explains predictive inference by integrating out regression parameters, then introduces ancestral sampling for directed graphical models and explains how it can produce samples from joint or marginal distributions. It describes generative models as graphical representations of how latent variables produce observations, illustrates this with object images determined by identity, position, and orientation, contrasts generative models with non-generative polynomial regression, and discusses the role of latent variables and synthetic data. It concludes by introducing discrete variables and the use of exponential-family distributions as components of complex models.

nodes.title: 8.1.3 Discrete variables
nodes.summary: The text introduces graphical models as representations of generative processes, explaining the roles of observed and latent variables through an object-image example and contrasting generative models with polynomial regression. It then develops directed models for discrete variables, deriving parameter counts for multinomial, joint, independent, fully connected, chain, and parameter-tied structures. It explains how graph sparsity and parameter sharing control exponential complexity, how Dirichlet priors extend these models into Bayesian networks, and how logistic-sigmoid parameterizations provide a more parsimonious but restricted alternative to complete conditional-probability tables.

nodes.title: 8.1.4 Linear-Gaussian models
nodes.summary: The text develops linear-Gaussian graphical models, showing that Gaussian conditionals whose means are linear functions of parent variables produce a multivariate Gaussian joint distribution. It gives noise-based representations and recursive formulas for means and covariances, examines independent, fully connected, and partially connected graphs, and explains how graph structure constrains covariance parameters. The formulation is extended to multivariate Gaussian nodes and related to Gaussian conjugate priors, hyperpriors, and hierarchical Bayesian models. The text then defines conditional independence and demonstrates its equivalent conditional factorization property.

This section introduces Bayesian networks as directed graphical models that factor joint distributions into node-specific conditional distributions given their parents. It explains graph structure, variable ordering, DAGs, missing links, normalization, and ancestral sampling, then applies the framework to Bayesian polynomial regression and generative modeling with latent variables. It develops discrete Bayesian networks, covering structures, parameter complexity, sparsity, parameter tying, Dirichlet priors, and logistic parameterizations, and develops linear-Gaussian networks, including their noise representations, moment calculations, covariance constraints, multivariate extensions, conjugate and hierarchical priors, and the concept of conditional independence.

nodes.title: 8.2. Conditional Independence
8.2.1 Three example graphs
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional independence and its shorthand notation, explains why graphical models are valuable for identifying such properties, and motivates d-separation. It analyzes three three-node directed graphs: a common cause and a chain, where conditioning on the middle node blocks dependence, and a collider, where conditioning on the middle node or its descendant creates dependence. The collider behavior is demonstrated numerically through a battery, fuel tank, and unreliable gauge example illustrating explaining away. Finally, it states the general d-separation criterion for node sets and paths in directed acyclic graphs, including the blocking rules for tail-to-tail, head-to-tail, and head-to-head nodes.

nodes.title: 8.2.2 D-separation
nodes.summary: The text explains how evidence can alter dependencies in a fuel-gauge example, including explaining away, and then presents d-separation as the graphical criterion for conditional independence in directed acyclic graphs. It gives the blocking rules for collider and non-collider paths, illustrates them with graphs, and applies them to parameter nodes, i.i.d. Gaussian observations, Bayesian regression, and the naive Bayes classifier. It discusses the benefits and limitations of naive Bayes, states the equivalence between directed factorization and d-separation, interprets graphs as filters defining families of distributions, and contrasts fully connected and disconnected graphs. It then defines the Markov blanket as a node's parents, children, and co-parents, before introducing undirected Markov random fields and their simpler graph-separation semantics.

This section extends graphical models to multivariate linear-Gaussian and hierarchical Bayesian constructions, then develops conditional independence and its factorization property. Through common-cause, chain, and collider examples—including explaining away—it motivates d-separation and gives its path-blocking rules for directed acyclic graphs. The section applies these ideas to Gaussian observations, Bayesian regression, parameter relationships, and naive Bayes, explains how graph structure constrains distributions, defines Markov blankets, and introduces the analogous separation semantics of undirected Markov random fields.

nodes.title: 8.3. Markov Random Fields
8.3.1 Conditional independence properties
nodes.summary: The text explains directed-graph Markov blankets and then introduces Markov random fields as undirected graphical models that encode factorization and conditional independence. In undirected graphs, conditional independence is determined by ordinary graph separation: A is independent of B given C when removing C disconnects A from B. This avoids the explaining-away complexities of d-separation. It also notes that an undirected node’s Markov blanket is its set of neighbors and begins developing the corresponding local factorization of the joint distribution.

nodes.title: 8.3.2 Factorization properties
nodes.summary: The text explains conditional independence and factorization in undirected graphical models. Independence between sets A and B given C is determined by graph separation: all A-to-B paths must pass through C, or equivalently no such path remains after removing C. This avoids the explaining-away issue of directed graphs, and each node’s Markov blanket is simply its neighbors. Nonconnected variables must not share a factor, motivating cliques and maximal cliques as the domains of factors. The joint distribution is represented as a normalized product of nonnegative clique potentials, with a partition function that may be exponentially costly to compute; unlike directed factors, these potentials have no required probabilistic interpretation. The partition function is important for learning, while it cancels in local conditionals and can be handled through explicit marginal normalization. For strictly positive potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem establishes equivalence between graph-separation independences and maximal-clique factorization. Potentials may be expressed exponentially through energy functions, forming a Boltzmann distribution whose configurations reflect competing local preferences. Finally, binary image denoising is introduced as an application involving noisy sign-flipped pixels and strong correlations between neighboring clean pixels.

nodes.title: 8.3.3 Illustration: Image de-noising
nodes.summary: The text explains the equivalence, for strictly positive distributions, between conditional-independence representations and maximal-clique factorizations in Markov random fields, introduces energy/Boltzmann formulations and the interpretation of clique potentials, and applies them to binary image de-noising. It defines unary, observation-agreement, and neighboring-pixel energies, the resulting joint and conditional distributions, and the Ising-model interpretation. It then describes ICM optimization, its local-maxima limitation, parameter settings and results, and contrasts it with max-product and globally optimal graph-cut methods. Finally, it begins showing how a directed chain can be represented by an equivalent undirected chain with pairwise potentials.

nodes.title: 8.3.4 Relation to directed graphs
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of image denoising by contrasting ICM, max-product, and globally optimal graph-cut methods, then explains how directed graphical models can be converted to undirected ones through factor absorption and moralization. It defines D maps, I maps, and perfect maps, shows that directed and undirected graphs express different conditional-independence structures, and introduces chain graphs as a broader but still non-universal framework. It finally introduces inference as posterior computation for unobserved nodes given clamped observations, emphasizing exploitation of graphical structure for efficiency.

This section develops Markov random fields as undirected graphical models whose conditional independences follow ordinary graph separation, with neighborhoods serving as Markov blankets. It explains clique and maximal-clique factorization, normalized clique potentials, partition functions, energy/Boltzmann forms, and the Hammersley–Clifford theorem. These ideas are applied to binary image denoising through an Ising-style model with unary and pairwise energies, using ICM, max-product, and graph-cut inference. The section then relates directed and undirected representations through factor absorption and moralization, compares their independence structures using D-maps, I-maps, and perfect maps, introduces chain graphs, and motivates efficient posterior inference from observed variables.

nodes.title: 8.4. Inference in Graphical Models
8.4.1 Inference on a chain
nodes.summary: The text introduces exact inference in graphical models through Bayes’ theorem and then develops sum-product message passing for an undirected chain. Naive marginalization of the full joint distribution is exponential, whereas exploiting factorization, distributivity, and conditional independence yields forward and backward recursive messages with O(NK²) cost. Node marginals are products of opposing messages normalized by Z; all marginals can be obtained efficiently by propagating and storing messages in both directions. The method also handles observed variables by clamping them, provides neighboring-node joint distributions and clique marginals, and supports EM parameter learning. Markov-chain and Chapman–Kolmogorov interpretations are noted, followed by an introduction to inference on trees.

nodes.title: 8.4.2 Trees
nodes.summary: The text explains how bidirectional message passing efficiently computes every marginal in a chain, including handling observed variables by clamping and indicator functions. It gives the neighboring-node joint distribution in terms of forward and backward messages, notes that all local clique or edge distributions become available after message passing, and explains their use in the EM algorithm for parameter learning with incomplete data. It then generalizes exact inference from chains to trees and polytrees, defining undirected trees, directed trees, and polytrees and discussing moralization. Finally, it introduces factor graphs as a general representation for the sum-product algorithm, explicitly expressing a joint distribution as a product of factors over variable subsets.

nodes.title: 8.4.3 Factor graphs
nodes.summary: The text explains why trees, directed trees, and polytrees permit efficient inference by local message passing, defining their structures and describing how moralization affects them. It introduces factor graphs as bipartite representations that explicitly encode products of factors, gives their mathematical form and examples, and explains conversions from directed and undirected graphs, including the nonuniqueness of such representations. Factor-graph conversion preserves tree structure even for directed polytrees and can eliminate apparent local cycles by combining factors. Finally, it introduces the sum-product algorithm for exact marginal inference on tree-structured graphs, noting its discrete summation form, continuous linear-Gaussian integration analogue, and extension to max-sum inference for finding the most probable state.

nodes.title: 8.4.4 The sum-product algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how factor graphs represent directed and undirected graphical models while retaining tree structure, then derives the sum-product algorithm for exact marginal inference. It defines factor-to-variable and variable-to-factor messages, leaf initialization, recursive propagation, efficient computation of all variable and factor marginals, normalization for undirected models, and illustrates the method with a four-variable example. It also covers conditioning on observed variables and extension to continuous models through integration. Finally, it introduces the max-sum algorithm for joint maximum-probability assignments, emphasizing why maximizing individual marginals is not equivalent to maximizing the joint distribution.

nodes.title: 8.4.5 The max-sum algorithm
nodes.summary: The text introduces max-sum inference as the dynamic-programming counterpart of sum-product for finding both the maximum value of a factorized joint distribution and the globally most probable variable configuration. It illustrates why maximizing marginals independently can fail, derives max-product and its logarithmic max-sum form using the distributive property, and gives message-passing rules for tree-structured graphs. It explains initialization, root maximization, the need to record maximizing predecessor states, and back-tracking to obtain a globally consistent solution, especially through a chain trellis. The method is exact on trees, becomes the Viterbi algorithm for hidden Markov models, handles evidence by clamping observed variables, and is contrasted with the simpler but non-globally-optimal ICM algorithm. The text also notes that continuous-variable sum-product operations use integrations and references linear-Gaussian systems for an example.

nodes.title: 8.4.6 Exact inference in general graphs
nodes.summary: The text explains exact inference in loopy graphical models through the junction tree algorithm: moralizing directed graphs, triangulating them, forming a maximum-spanning join tree of maximal cliques, enforcing the running intersection property, and using message passing to compute marginals and conditionals. It emphasizes that the method is exact but can be exponentially costly in the largest clique, with treewidth measuring this complexity. It then introduces loopy belief propagation as an approximate extension of sum-product inference to cyclic graphs, describing its local message updates, possible convergence failure, unit-message initialization, flooding and serial schedules, and the use of pending messages to organize updates.

nodes.title: 8.4.7 Loopy belief propagation
nodes.summary: The text explains treewidth and why large clique sizes make junction-tree inference infeasible, then introduces loopy belief propagation as a local sum-product approximation for cyclic graphs, including initialization, pending-message rules, flooding and serial schedules, convergence behavior, marginal computation, and applications to error-correcting codes. It next discusses Bayesian learning of graph structures, posterior scoring, evidence computation, and the exponential search problem. Two exercises concern normalization of directed-graph factorizations and the ordering characterization of acyclic directed graphs.

nodes.title: 8.4.8 Learning the graph structure
nodes.summary: The text explains termination and accuracy of belief propagation on trees, convergence and approximate marginals in loopy graphs, and its mixed performance, including success in error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces learning graphical-model structure from data, describing Bayesian posterior scoring with model evidence and the computational difficulties caused by latent-variable marginalization and exponentially many candidate graphs. Two exercises address normalization of directed-graph factorizations and the relationship between node ordering and the absence of directed cycles.

This section develops inference in graphical models from exact message passing on chains and trees to factor-graph formulations, sum-product marginalization, and max-sum global optimization. It covers observations, continuous variables, EM-related local marginals, directed trees and polytrees, and the Viterbi algorithm. For general graphs it presents junction-tree inference, moralization, triangulation, treewidth, and exact clique propagation, followed by loopy belief propagation as an approximate method with convergence and scheduling considerations. The section also discusses graphical-model representation limits through perfect maps and chain graphs, and introduces Bayesian learning of graph structure, including model evidence, latent variables, and computational complexity.

nodes.title: 8.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text explains termination and marginal computation for belief propagation on trees and loopy graphs, noting its variable performance and application to error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of graph structures, including posterior scoring, evidence-computation difficulties, and heuristic search over exponentially many structures. Two exercises concern proving normalization of a directed-graph factorization and deriving acyclicity from a suitable node ordering.

nodes.title: 8.2 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of belief propagation by contrasting exact termination and marginals on trees with potentially nonterminating but often effective loopy belief propagation, including its use in error-correcting-code decoding. It then introduces Bayesian learning of unknown graph structures, describing posterior scoring by prior times model evidence and the computational challenges of latent-variable marginalization and exponentially large structure spaces. The remaining content lists Exercises 8.1–8.9, covering normalization and acyclicity of directed graphical models, marginal and conditional independence using a binary-variable table, directed-model factorization and graph construction, the relevance vector machine, interpretation of the noisy-OR model, Gaussian mean and covariance recursions, implications of conditional independence, and the Markov-blanket property via d-separation.

nodes.summary: The text presents a joint distribution for three binary variables and a set of exercises on probabilistic graphical models. The exercises cover verifying marginal dependence and conditional independence, deriving conditional and marginal distributions and a graph factorization, constructing a graphical model for a relevance vector machine, interpreting the noisy-OR model and its parameters, deriving Gaussian means and covariances from recursion relations, proving a conditional-independence property, and establishing the Markov blanket conditional-independence result using d-separation.

nodes.summary: The text presents a joint probability table for three binary variables and a set of graphical-model exercises covering direct checks of marginal and conditional independence, conditional-distribution evaluation and graph factorization, construction of a relevance-vector-machine graphical model, interpretation of the noisy-OR model and its background parameter, derivation of Gaussian mean and covariance recursions, a conditional-independence implication, and the Markov-blanket property established through d-separation.

nodes.title: 8.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 8.3–8.15 on graphical models, conditional independence, Bayesian-network factorization, noisy-OR models, recursive Gaussian moments, d-separation and Markov blankets, explaining-away effects, graph enumeration, local energy differences and ICM, special cases of latent-variable energies, and pairwise distributions in neighboring graphical-model nodes. It includes a joint-distribution table for three binary variables, references to several figures and equations, and asks for direct probability calculations, proofs, graphical constructions, interpretations, and derivations.

nodes.summary: The text presents a graphical-model example involving conditional independence and how observing a descendant can activate a head-to-head path, followed by exercises on this phenomenon and its application to an unreliable fuel-gauge report, enumeration of undirected graphs, locality of energy changes in iterated conditional modes, the maximum-probability configuration when interaction and bias terms vanish, and the joint distribution of neighboring nodes in a graphical model.

nodes.title: 8.15 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents Exercises 8.10–8.24 on graphical models, covering d-separation and the effect of conditioning on collider descendants, probabilistic reasoning with noisy observations, enumeration of undirected graphs, local energy changes and maximum-probability configurations, tree-structured distributions, and efficient inference through message passing. The exercises develop sum-product algorithms for chains and factor graphs, message-ordering proofs, computation of variable and factor marginals, connected-subset marginals, equivalence between directed and undirected trees, and alternative expressions for message-based marginals.

nodes.title: 8.18 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 8.16–8.29 examine message passing and sum-product inference in directed and factor trees. They cover efficient conditional inference, d-separation and irrelevance of observed variables, equivalence between directed and undirected tree representations, recovery of chain-model formulas, valid message scheduling by induction, computation of variable-set and factor marginals, alternative marginal expressions using incoming and outgoing messages, verification of marginal and joint results on an example graph, clamping-based computation of pairwise distributions, a counterexample showing marginal modes need not form a joint mode, and the relationship between pending messages and graph structure: cycles preserve pending messages, whereas finite message passing on trees eliminates them.

This section presents probabilistic graphical models as diagrammatic tools for representing, analyzing, and inferring probability distributions. It develops Bayesian networks and linear-Gaussian models, conditional independence and d-separation, Markov random fields and their energy-based clique factorizations, and the relationships between directed, undirected, and chain-graph representations. It then covers exact message passing, sum-product and max-sum inference, Viterbi decoding, junction trees, treewidth, loopy belief propagation, observations and continuous variables, and Bayesian learning of graph structures. Applications include regression, latent-variable generation, naive Bayes, image denoising, and error-correcting codes, while exercises reinforce independence reasoning, graph construction, Gaussian recursions, energy methods, graph enumeration, and message-passing algorithms.

nodes.title: 9 Mixture Models and EM
9.1. K -means Clustering
9.1.1 Image segmentation and compression
nodes.summary: The text extends K-means to K-medoids using arbitrary dissimilarities, describing its hard-assignment E step, prototype-based M step, and computational costs, then motivates probabilistic soft clustering for ambiguous points. It illustrates K-means in image segmentation, where pixels are clustered by RGB values, and in lossy vector-quantization compression, including the storage formula, numerical example, compression ratios, quality trade-off, and the benefit of clustering pixel blocks. Finally, it introduces Gaussian mixtures as richer density models represented with 1-of-K latent variables, defining their mixture density, joint-distribution construction, and relationship between latent states and mixing coefficients.

This section develops K-means clustering as an alternating optimization of hard point-to-cluster assignments and cluster means under a squared-distance distortion objective. It explains the E and M steps, convergence and local-minimum limitations, and illustrates the algorithm on standardized Old Faithful data. It then discusses K-medoids for arbitrary dissimilarities, the motivation for probabilistic soft assignments, and applications of K-means to image segmentation and lossy vector-quantization compression, including storage and quality trade-offs and block-based improvements. Finally, it motivates Gaussian mixture models, introducing their 1-of-K latent variables, mixture density, joint distribution, and mixing coefficients.

nodes.title: 9.2. Mixtures of Gaussians
9.2.1 Maximum likelihood
nodes.summary: The text explains posterior component responsibilities in Gaussian mixtures, their prior interpretation, and how they support sampling and visualization of complete, incomplete, and responsibility-labeled data. It formulates the mixture likelihood for i.i.d. observations and discusses major maximum-likelihood difficulties: covariance-collapse singularities, overfitting, heuristic remedies, and label-switching identifiability. Because the likelihood lacks closed-form optimization due to a sum inside the logarithm, the text introduces EM as a general latent-variable optimization method and derives the responsibility-weighted update for each Gaussian component mean, based on the effective membership count N_k.

nodes.title: 9.2.2 EM for Gaussian mixtures
EM for Gaussian Mixtures
nodes.summary: The text explains Gaussian-mixture EM through an iterative visualization and formal algorithm. Responsibilities softly assign points to components, while the M step updates each component’s weighted mean, covariance, and mixing coefficient; repeated cycles approach convergence. Because EM is slower and costlier than K-means, K-means is commonly used for initialization, though singular likelihoods must be avoided and EM may reach only a local maximum. The complete procedure alternates responsibility computation, parameter re-estimation, and likelihood-based convergence checks. It then introduces an alternative latent-variable perspective, defining observed data, latent variables, and parameters, noting that the likelihood sums or integrates the joint distribution over latent variables inside a logarithm.

This section derives and motivates EM for Gaussian mixtures. Responsibilities provide soft component assignments and determine effective component sizes, weighted means, covariances, and mixing coefficients. Because these quantities depend on one another, EM alternates an E step that computes responsibilities with an M step that re-estimates parameters; each cycle increases the likelihood until convergence. The procedure is illustrated on Old Faithful data, with K-means commonly useful for initialization, while singular solutions and local maxima remain concerns. The discussion also introduces EM’s broader latent-variable perspective, in which marginal likelihoods involve summing or integrating over unobserved variables.

This section introduces Gaussian mixtures as latent-variable models in which a 1-of-K component indicator selects one of several Gaussian distributions, and shows that marginalizing this indicator gives the usual mixture density. It develops posterior responsibilities and their interpretation, formulates maximum-likelihood estimation, and explains difficulties including singular covariances, overfitting, label switching, and the absence of a closed-form solution. These motivate EM, which alternates responsibility computation with responsibility-weighted updates of component sizes, means, covariances, and mixing coefficients, increasing likelihood until convergence. The method is illustrated on Old Faithful data, with K-means initialization and remaining risks of local maxima and singularities, while also motivating EM more generally for latent-variable models. The opening context additionally relates clustering to image compression and its compression-quality trade-off.

nodes.title: 9.3. An Alternative View of EM
The General EM Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text introduces EM as a method for maximizing likelihoods involving latent or missing variables. It contrasts incomplete observed data with hypothetical complete data, defines the posterior-based expected complete-data log likelihood Q, and presents the iterative E-step/M-step algorithm, including initialization, parameter updates, convergence, and its monotonic likelihood-improvement property. It also explains the MAP extension using a parameter prior, the use of EM for missing-at-random data, and the beginning of its application to Gaussian mixture models, where hidden component labels make direct likelihood optimization difficult.

nodes.title: 9.3.1 Gaussian mixtures revisited
nodes.summary: The text presents the general EM procedure, including its E and M steps, convergence check, and extension to MAP estimation through parameter priors. It explains how EM handles missing data under a missing-at-random assumption and introduces Gaussian mixtures from the complete-data perspective: the complete-data likelihood becomes separable, yielding simple estimates for component parameters and mixing weights. Since component labels are latent, their posterior expectations—responsibilities—are used to form the expected complete-data log likelihood, whose alternating evaluation and maximization reproduce the standard Gaussian-mixture EM updates. The section concludes by contrasting EM’s soft assignments with K-means’ hard assignments and noting that K-means arises as a limiting case of EM with shared isotropic covariances.

nodes.title: 9.3.2 Relation to K -means
nodes.summary: The text derives the posterior responsibilities and expected complete-data log likelihood for Gaussian-mixture EM, explains the E and M steps and their closed-form parameter updates, and then shows that K-means is obtained as the zero-variance limit of EM with shared isotropic covariances: soft responsibilities become hard nearest-mean assignments, the mean updates become the K-means updates, and the likelihood objective becomes the K-means distortion objective. It also notes elliptical K-means as a general-covariance hard-assignment variant and introduces Bernoulli mixture models, or latent class analysis, as an important discrete-variable application and precursor to hidden Markov models.

nodes.title: 9.3.3 Mixtures of Bernoulli distributions
nodes.summary: The text shows that EM for isotropic Gaussian mixtures becomes K-means in the zero-variance limit, producing hard nearest-mean assignments, K-means mean updates, cluster-fraction mixing coefficients, and the K-means distortion objective; it also notes the elliptical K-means generalization. It then develops mixtures of independent Bernoulli distributions, deriving their moments, likelihood, latent-variable formulation, complete-data objective, responsibility calculation, and EM updates for component parameters and mixing coefficients. Bernoulli mixtures can model correlations, lack Gaussian-mixture-style infinite likelihood singularities, and are demonstrated on binarized handwritten digits. The discussion also covers beta and Dirichlet priors and multinomial extensions, and introduces EM for Bayesian linear regression evidence approximation by treating the weights as latent variables and re-estimating the hyperparameters alpha and beta.

nodes.title: 9.3.4 EM for Bayesian linear regression
nodes.summary: The text presents Bernoulli mixture models for binarized digits, including visualization, comparison with a single Bernoulli model, priors, and multinomial extensions. It then applies EM to Bayesian linear regression and relevance vector machines by treating weights as latent variables, deriving updates for α and β, and showing their equivalence to evidence-maximization updates. Finally, it introduces the general EM framework for observed variables X and latent variables Z, expressing the log likelihood as a lower-bound functional plus a KL divergence and explaining why complete-data optimization can simplify latent-variable maximum likelihood.

This section develops EM from both algorithmic and conceptual perspectives. It describes its likelihood and MAP forms, handling of missing data, and convergence procedure; applies it to Gaussian mixtures with responsibility-based parameter updates; derives K-means as a zero-variance hard-assignment limit; and extends the method to Bernoulli and multinomial mixtures, including digit modeling and priors. It also applies EM to Bayesian linear regression and relevance vector machines, and concludes with the general lower-bound/KL-divergence interpretation that explains EM’s alternating E- and M-steps.

nodes.title: 9.4. The EM Algorithm in General
nodes.summary: The text develops the general EM algorithm from a variational lower-bound decomposition of the latent-variable log likelihood. It defines the bound and KL divergence, proves the E and M steps and their monotonic likelihood improvement, explains their relation to expected complete-data likelihood, exponential-family models, Gaussian-mixture responsibilities, and parameter-space geometry, and extends the method to MAP estimation, GEM, ECM, partial E steps, and incremental EM with sufficient-statistic updates. It concludes with exercises on finite K-means convergence and stochastic K-means via Robbins–Monro.

The method has constant per-step cost, may converge faster than batch EM, and preserves the relationship between maxima of the auxiliary function and likelihood. Two exercises address finite convergence of K-means and deriving stochastic K-means via Robbins–Monro estimation.

This section introduces mixture models as latent-variable constructions obtained by marginalization and develops their use for clustering, beginning with K-means, its optimization behavior, variants, and compression applications. It then presents Gaussian mixtures, latent component indicators, responsibilities, maximum-likelihood difficulties, and the EM algorithm for estimating component parameters. EM is developed through likelihood, MAP, missing-data, variational lower-bound, KL-divergence, and expected-complete-data perspectives, with extensions to generalized, constrained, partial, and incremental forms. Applications include Bernoulli and multinomial mixtures, digit modeling, Bayesian linear regression, and relevance vector machines. The exercises reinforce Gaussian and Bernoulli mixture derivations, MAP-EM, posterior factorization, constrained updates, conditional mixtures, mixture moments, K-means limits, likelihood boundedness, Bayesian and variational interpretations, and stochastic or incremental EM.

nodes.title: 10 Approximate Inference
10.1. Variational Inference
10.1.1 Factorized distributions
Leonhard Euler
nodes.summary: The text derives mean-field variational inference for a factorized approximation: maximizing the lower bound with respect to one factor reduces to minimizing a KL divergence, giving an optimal factor whose log equals the expectation of the joint log distribution over all other factors plus a normalization constant. Because the factor updates are mutually dependent, they are solved by cyclic coordinate updates, with convergence ensured by separate convexity. The text then introduces the properties and inaccuracies of factorized approximations through a correlated two-variable Gaussian example, and includes a biographical note on Leonhard Euler and his mathematical achievements.

The section introduces factorized variational distributions as a tractable restriction of the posterior approximation family, contrasts them with parameterized approaches, derives the coordinate-wise optimal factor updates and their cyclic solution, and discusses convergence and approximation inaccuracies using a correlated Gaussian example. It also contains a biographical note about Leonhard Euler.

nodes.title: 10.1.2 Properties of factorized approximations
nodes.summary: The text derives coordinate-wise optimal updates for factorized variational inference and explains their iterative implementation and convergence. It analyzes the resulting approximation using a correlated Gaussian, showing that factorization preserves the mean but generally underestimates uncertainty. It compares the behaviors of KL(q||p) and KL(p||q), including their effects on Gaussian and multimodal approximations, then generalizes the discussion to alpha-divergences and their zero-forcing or zero-avoiding properties. Finally, it sets up a univariate Gaussian mean-and-precision inference example using conjugate Gaussian-Gamma priors and a factorized variational posterior.

nodes.title: 10.1.3 Example: The univariate Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text discusses alpha-divergences, their KL and Hellinger special cases, and the contrasting zero-forcing and zero-avoiding behavior obtained when approximating a fixed distribution. It then develops a factorized variational approximation for the posterior of the mean and precision of a univariate Gaussian: starting from the Gaussian likelihood and Gaussian-Gamma conjugate priors, it derives Gaussian and Gamma optimal factors, explains their mutually dependent moments and coordinate-update procedure, illustrates convergence against the true posterior, and begins an explicit solution under noninformative priors.

This section introduces variational inference as optimization over probability distributions, explains the calculus-of-variations foundations and the evidence lower bound/KL-divergence decomposition, and shows that the unrestricted optimum is the exact posterior. It then develops factorized variational approximations, their coordinate updates and convergence, and analyzes their limitations through correlated Gaussian examples, including underestimated uncertainty. The section compares alternative KL directions and alpha-divergences, discusses zero-forcing and zero-avoiding behavior, and applies the framework to Gaussian mean-and-precision inference with conjugate Gaussian-Gamma priors, deriving the factor distributions, iterative dependencies, convergence behavior, and an initial noninformative-prior solution.

This section motivates approximate inference for otherwise intractable posterior distributions and expectations, then develops variational inference through variational optimization, the ELBO, and KL divergence. It establishes the exact-posterior optimum, presents factorized approximations and coordinate updates, analyzes convergence and uncertainty underestimation in correlated Gaussian settings, compares divergence choices and their support behavior, and applies the method to Gaussian mean-and-precision inference with conjugate and noninformative priors.

This appendix surveys probabilistic and statistical learning foundations from Gaussian distributions through modern models and inference methods. It develops Gaussian geometry, conditioning, marginalization, Bayes’ theorem, maximum-likelihood, sequential, and conjugate Bayesian estimation; Student’s t and periodic distributions; mixtures, exponential-family theory, and nonparametric density estimation. It includes extensive exercises on probability, distributions, entropy, KL divergence, matrix and Gaussian identities, and estimation. The later material covers linear regression and classification, Bayesian evidence, neural networks, kernel methods, Gaussian processes, sparse SVM and relevance-vector machines, graphical models and message passing, mixture models and EM, and variational approximate inference, including their optimization, uncertainty, computational, and model-selection issues.

nodes.title: Appendix B
10.1.4 Model comparison
nodes.summary: The text first derives the variational moments for a Gaussian mean and precision, showing that the resulting posterior precision estimate is the unbiased sample variance, unlike the maximum-likelihood estimate. It then develops variational model comparison for models with potentially different latent-variable structures, using q(Z,m)=q(Z|m)q(m), a lower-bound/KL decomposition, and q(m) proportional to p(m) exp(L_m); latent distributions are optimized per model before model selection or averaging. Finally, it begins a variational treatment of Bayesian Gaussian mixtures, defining the latent assignments, mixture likelihood terms, use of precision matrices, and a symmetric Dirichlet conjugate prior over mixing coefficients.

nodes.title: 10.2. Illustration: Variational Mixture of Gaussians
10.2.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian inference for a conjugate Gaussian mixture model. It specifies the graphical model and priors, distinguishes latent assignments from fixed parameters, derives the factorized variational posterior, responsibilities, weighted sufficient statistics, and Dirichlet and Gaussian-Wishart parameter updates, and gives the required distributional expectations. The resulting iterative procedure parallels EM while incorporating Bayesian parameter uncertainty and automatic component selection. Applications to Old Faithful illustrate how the Dirichlet hyperparameter controls inactive components. The method has EM-like computational cost, avoids maximum-likelihood singularities and overfitting, and can determine the effective number of components. Finally, the text introduces the variational lower bound, its decomposition into likelihood, prior, and entropy terms, and its use for convergence and implementation checks.

nodes.title: 10.2.2 Variational lower bound
nodes.summary: The passage explains the benefits of Bayesian and variational Gaussian mixtures, including removal of likelihood singularities, avoidance of overfitting with many components, and automatic selection of model complexity. It presents the variational lower bound as a convergence and implementation diagnostic, gives its decomposition and explicit component terms for the Gaussian-mixture model, and notes that entropy terms can be combined. It also describes deriving the update equations by maximizing this bound under conjugate variational distributions, and introduces the predictive density for a new observation by integrating over its latent assignment, weights, and component parameters.

nodes.title: 10.2.3 Predictive density
nodes.summary: The text completes the variational lower-bound expressions for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture, explains their entropy terms and their use in deriving variational updates, then derives the variational predictive density as a mixture of Student's t-distributions that approaches a Gaussian mixture for large samples. It finally begins the discussion of selecting the number of components, emphasizing the K! label-switching-equivalent parameterizations and why this symmetry is inconsequential for maximum likelihood but important for Bayesian marginalization.

nodes.title: 10.2.4 Determining the number of components
nodes.summary: The text derives the variational predictive density for a Gaussian mixture as a mixture of Student’s t-distributions that becomes approximately Gaussian with large data sets. It discusses selecting the number of components, accounting for K! label-switching modes with an ln K! correction, the Old Faithful example, and the contrast between Bayesian model comparison and maximum likelihood. It also presents an alternative sparsity-based approach that optimizes mixing coefficients and prunes unnecessary components. Finally, it explains induced factorizations in variational posteriors, their computational importance, and their detection through conditional independence and d-separation.

nodes.title: 10.2.5 Induced factorizations
nodes.summary: The text explains automatic relevance determination for pruning irrelevant Gaussian-mixture components, then develops the concept of induced factorizations in variational inference. It shows how optimal posterior factors split across mixture components and observations, derives a general conditional-independence criterion using d-separation, and applies it to the Gaussian-mixture graph. It then introduces variational Bayesian linear regression, contrasting it with evidence-based point estimation, fixing the noise precision for simplicity, specifying the likelihood, Gaussian weight prior, gamma hyperprior on the precision, joint distribution, graphical model, and goal of approximating the posterior over weights and precision.

This section develops variational Bayesian inference for Gaussian mixtures from their latent-variable likelihood and conjugate priors through factorized posterior updates, responsibilities, sufficient statistics, and Gaussian-Wishart and Dirichlet parameter estimation. It explains the variational lower bound and its use for updates, convergence, and diagnostics; derives a Student's t mixture predictive density; and addresses component-number selection through Bayesian comparison, label-switching corrections, and automatic sparsity-based pruning. The discussion also explains induced posterior factorizations via conditional independence and d-separation, and transitions to variational Bayesian linear regression as a further application.

nodes.title: 10.3. Variational Linear Regression
10.3.1 Variational distribution
nodes.summary: The passage first notes how d-separation verifies variational factorization in a Gaussian mixture model, then develops variational Bayesian linear regression with known noise precision, a Gaussian weight prior, and a gamma prior on its precision. Assuming q(w, α) = q(w)q(α), it derives gamma and Gaussian update equations, their moments, and an alternating optimization procedure. It shows that with an infinitely broad hyperprior, the variational solution agrees with evidence maximization/EM, and concludes by deriving the Gaussian predictive distribution for a new input, including both observation noise and posterior parameter uncertainty.

nodes.title: 10.3.2 Predictive distribution
nodes.summary: The text derives the variational Gaussian posterior for linear-regression weights and the required moments, explains alternating updates of q(w) and q(alpha), and shows that under a noninformative alpha prior the variational result coincides with evidence maximization by EM when alpha estimates are replaced by their expectations. It derives the Gaussian predictive distribution with input-dependent variance, defines and expands the variational lower bound into likelihood, prior, and entropy terms, and demonstrates that using this bound for polynomial model selection correctly favors the degree-three model while avoiding the overfitting tendency of maximum likelihood.

nodes.title: 10.3.3 Lower bound
nodes.summary: The passage completes variational linear regression by giving its predictive variance and the explicit variational lower bound, including all expected likelihood, prior, and entropy terms. It explains how the bound supports Bayesian model selection, correctly choosing the true polynomial order in an example and avoiding the overfitting tendency of maximum likelihood. It then introduces exponential-family modeling for IID observed and latent variables, distinguishes extensive latent variables from fixed-dimensional parameters, presents the joint exponential-family form and its conjugate prior, and begins the corresponding variational framework.

This section develops variational Bayesian linear regression by deriving factorized Gaussian and gamma posterior updates, their moments, alternating optimization, and the relationship to evidence maximization and EM. It obtains the uncertainty-aware Gaussian predictive distribution and an explicit variational lower bound comprising likelihood, prior, and entropy contributions. The bound enables effective Bayesian polynomial model selection without maximum-likelihood overfitting. The section concludes by introducing exponential-family representations, conjugate priors, and the initial variational treatment for IID observed and latent-variable models.

nodes.title: 10.4. Exponential Family Distributions
10.4.1 Variational message passing
nodes.summary: The text derives mean-field variational updates for an exponential-family model, showing that the latent factors separate by data point while the parameter posterior retains a conjugate exponential-family form with updated hyperparameters. These coupled factors are optimized through alternating variational E and M steps. It then generalizes the method to directed graphical models, where factor updates are local to each node's Markov blanket. In conjugate-exponential networks, the updates become variational message passing between parents, children, and co-parents, which also facilitates lower-bound evaluation and provides a scalable basis for general-purpose inference.

The section develops variational inference for models whose complete-data distributions and conjugate parameter priors are in the exponential family. It distinguishes latent variables from fixed-dimensional parameters, derives separable latent and conjugate parameter variational factors with alternating E- and M-step optimization, and generalizes the resulting local updates to variational message passing in directed conjugate-exponential graphical models, including efficient lower-bound computation and scalable inference.

nodes.title: 10.5. Local Variational Methods
nodes.summary: The text develops local variational inference through convex duality and tangent-based bounds. It derives the general conjugate representations for convex and concave functions, works out the example exp(-x), and applies transformed-function duality to obtain entropy-based exponential upper and Gaussian-form quadratic lower bounds for the logistic sigmoid. It explains how these bounds make otherwise intractable sigmoid-Gaussian integrals analytically tractable after optimizing a variational parameter, while noting that the optimized result is generally only an approximation. The section then introduces variational Bayesian logistic regression, emphasizing its Gaussian posterior approximation and rigorous evidence lower bound, and begins deriving the variational posterior using a Gaussian prior and the local sigmoid bound.

nodes.title: 10.6. Variational Logistic Regression
10.6.1 Variational posterior distribution
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using Jaakkola–Jordan’s local quadratic lower bound on the logistic sigmoid. Each observation receives a variational parameter, producing a quadratic lower bound on the likelihood and, with a Gaussian prior, a Gaussian variational posterior whose mean and precision are given explicitly. The approach improves flexibility and accuracy over the Laplace approximation while optimizing a rigorous evidence lower bound. The variational parameters are optimized either through EM or direct maximization after integrating out the weights; the excerpt begins the EM procedure. Batch and sequential use are discussed, along with the limitation that the binary-class bound does not directly generalize to multiclass problems.

nodes.title: 10.6.2 Optimizing the variational parameters
nodes.summary: The text develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using a quadratic bound, producing a Gaussian posterior whose parameters depend on local variational variables. It explains optimization of these variables through EM or equivalent analytical maximization, provides the update equations and closed-form evidence lower bound, and discusses batch and sequential learning, binary-class limitations, predictive inference, and illustrative large-margin behavior. It concludes by introducing variational inference of the prior hyperparameter α through a combined global-local framework.

nodes.title: 10.6.3 Inference of hyperparameters
nodes.summary: The text illustrates variational Bayesian logistic regression and its uncertainty behavior, including sequential updating and large-margin-like decision boundaries. It then develops variational inference for the prior precision hyperparameter α using a gamma hyperprior: a factorized approximation yields Gaussian and gamma posterior factors for the weights and α, respectively, together with iterative updates for the local parameters and required moments. Finally, it introduces expectation propagation, explaining that minimizing reverse KL divergence within an exponential family leads to matching the approximate and target distributions' expected sufficient statistics.

This section develops variational Bayesian logistic regression using the Jaakkola–Jordan quadratic likelihood bound, deriving Gaussian weight posteriors and methods for optimizing local variational parameters through EM or direct evidence maximization. It covers evidence bounds, batch and sequential learning, prediction, large-margin behavior, and binary-class limitations, then extends inference to the prior precision hyperparameter with a gamma model and concludes with the principles of expectation propagation and moment matching.

nodes.title: 10.7. Expectation Propagation
Expectation Propagation
nodes.summary: The text completes the EP factor-update derivation, showing that the normalization constant is obtained by zeroth-moment matching and equals the tilted-distribution integral. It then states the full Expectation Propagation algorithm for approximating posterior distributions and model evidence through iterative cavity distributions, moment matching, and factor replacement. It explains assumed density filtering as a one-pass EP special case, contrasts EP’s batch reuse of data with ADF’s order dependence, and discusses EP’s lack of guaranteed convergence, energy-function interpretation, direct optimization alternative, and differing KL objective from variational Bayes. EP may perform poorly for multimodal mixtures but often works well for logistic models. Finally, it introduces the Gaussian clutter problem, whose exact posterior has exponentially many mixture components, and specifies its mixture likelihood, Gaussian prior, EP factorization, spherical Gaussian approximation, parameters, and illustrative figure.

nodes.title: 10.7.1 Example: The clutter problem
nodes.summary: The text presents EP through a Gaussian-mixture clutter problem in which the mean of a target distribution must be inferred despite background observations. It specifies the likelihood, prior, parameter settings, and the exponentially large exact posterior, then develops the EP approximation using spherical Gaussian posterior and factor terms. It explains initialization, cavity construction, tilted-distribution normalization, moment matching, interpretation of the non-clutter probability, factor refinement, convergence, and evidence evaluation. It also discusses the behavior and visualization of factor approximations, including potentially negative factor variance parameters, compares EP with other approximations, and introduces the extension of EP to factor graphs with factors over variable subsets.

nodes.title: 10.7.2 Expectation propagation on graphs
nodes.summary: The text concludes the EP discussion by describing convergence, approximate evidence evaluation, unusual factor variances, and empirical comparisons with variational Bayes and Laplace methods. It then shows that EP on factor graphs with a fully factorized approximation is equivalent to loopy belief propagation: factor updates are obtained by removing an approximation, inserting the exact factor, marginalizing, and forming outgoing messages. Sequential updates reproduce standard belief propagation and are exact on trees. The general message-update rule is derived, and extensions using partially disconnected approximations or grouped factors are noted. Finally, EP and variational message passing are placed within a common alpha-divergence framework, and exercises review KL decompositions, moment matching, mean-field updates, and Gaussian approximation.

The section finishes the preceding variational Bayes updates and then develops expectation propagation as reverse-KL approximate inference. It derives exponential-family moment matching, factorized posterior and evidence approximations, cavity and tilted distributions, iterative factor replacement, normalization, and evidence estimation, while discussing assumed density filtering, convergence, optimization interpretations, and differences from variational Bayes. A Gaussian clutter problem illustrates EP in detail, including its posterior and factor approximations, moment updates, convergence, evidence, and unusual factor parameters. The section then extends EP to factor graphs, establishes its connection with loopy belief propagation and exactness on trees, gives general message updates and extensions, and relates EP and variational message passing through alpha-divergences.

nodes.summary: The passage explains how sum-product message passing emerges from expectation propagation under a fully factorized approximation, gives the corresponding factor-to-variable message computation, and discusses accuracy improvements through partially disconnected graphs and grouped-factor updates. It highlights the open problem of selecting the best grouping and disconnection structure, then presents the alpha-divergence framework unifying several message-passing algorithms. The section concludes with four exercises on KL-divergence decomposition, moment equations for factor means, variational-factor optimization using Lagrange multipliers, and Gaussian KL approximation, with the final exercise statement incomplete.

nodes.title: 10.3 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text explains the factor-node sum-product update and its interpretation as a fully factorized form of expectation propagation, then discusses more accurate partially connected or grouped-factor approximations and the unifying role of alpha-divergences across message-passing algorithms. It follows with exercises covering variational-bound and KL decompositions, moment matching, factorized variational updates, Gaussian KL projection, the EM connection, alpha-divergence limits, variational inference for Gaussian mean and precision, asymptotic behavior, expected precision, model inference bounds, constrained optimization over model probabilities, and the latent-variable posterior update for Bayesian Gaussian mixtures.

nodes.title: 10.5 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text states the moment-matching result obtained by minimizing KL(p‖q), then presents exercises on the equivalence between point-estimate variational inference and EM, limiting forms of the alpha divergence, variational Gaussian and gamma factors for estimating a Gaussian mean and precision, their large-sample behavior and expected-precision relation, the variational model-posterior decomposition, optimization of model probabilities under a normalization constraint, and derivation of the optimal latent-variable factor for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture.

nodes.title: 10.10 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text states the moment-matching result obtained by minimizing KL(p‖q), then presents exercises on the equivalence between factorized variational inference with point-estimated parameters and EM, limiting forms of the alpha divergence, variational Gaussian and gamma factors for unknown mean and precision, their large-sample behavior and expected-precision identity, variational model-posterior decomposition and optimization under normalization, and derivation of the optimal latent-variable distribution for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model.

nodes.title: 10.11 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text first states that KL minimization over a Gaussian approximation matches its mean and covariance to the expectation and covariance under the target distribution. It then presents exercises covering the equivalence between factorized variational inference with point-estimated parameters and EM, the limiting relationships between alpha divergences and the two KL divergences, derivation of Gaussian and gamma variational factors for univariate Gaussian inference, their large-sample behavior, and the reciprocal expected precision. Further exercises require deriving the variational model-posterior decomposition, the normalized optimum for q(m) using a Lagrange multiplier, and the optimal latent-variable variational distribution for a Bayesian Gaussian mixture.

nodes.summary: Exercises 10.13–10.21 develop and verify the variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model. They derive posterior distributions and parameters for component means, precisions, and mixing coefficients; verify expected values, lower-bound terms, and predictive distributions; obtain variational re-estimation equations directly from the lower bound; analyze the large-sample convergence of variational posteriors and responsibilities to the maximum-likelihood EM solution, with the predictive distribution reducing to a Gaussian mixture; and establish that component-label permutations create K! equivalent parameter settings.

nodes.title: 10.14 ( ) Using the distribution (10.59), verify the result (10.64).
nodes.summary: Exercises 10.13–10.21 develop and verify the variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model: deriving posterior factors and parameters, expected mixing coefficients, lower-bound terms, and variational re-estimation equations; deriving the predictive distribution; proving that the large-sample variational solution converges to the EM maximum-likelihood solution with Gaussian-mixture predictions; and counting K! equivalent parameter settings caused by component-label permutations.

nodes.title: 10.16 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 10.13–10.21 ask for derivations and verifications concerning the variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, including the optimal posterior factors, expected mixing coefficients, lower-bound terms, and re-estimation equations; derivation of the predictive distribution; demonstration that the large-sample variational solution converges to the maximum-likelihood EM solution, with responsibilities and predictive distribution having the corresponding limits; and calculation of the K! equivalent parameter settings caused by component permutations.

nodes.summary: Exercises 10.13–10.39 develop and verify variational and expectation-propagation methods across Bayesian Gaussian mixtures, Bayesian linear and logistic regression, and the clutter model. They derive variational posterior factors, responsibilities, predictive distributions, lower bounds, parameter re-estimation equations, exponential-family formulations, large-sample connections to maximum likelihood, symmetry effects, and evidence corrections. They also analyze MAP singularities and factorization-induced model-selection bias, extend regression with a gamma hyperprior, establish concavity-based variational bounds, derive sequential logistic-regression updates, and verify ADF and EP evidence, moment, cavity, normalization, and site-update formulas.

nodes.title: 11 Sampling Methods
11.1. Basic Sampling Algorithms
11.1.1 Standard distributions
nodes.summary: The text introduces basic sampling algorithms, beginning with pseudo-random uniform number generation and the transformation method for converting uniform samples into samples from specified distributions. It derives the method through the change-of-variables formula and inverse cumulative distribution, illustrating it with exponential and Cauchy distributions, extending it using Jacobians, and detailing the Box-Muller construction of standard and multivariate Gaussian samples, including Cholesky-based covariance transformation. Because inverse integrals are usually unavailable for complex distributions, the text then motivates rejection and importance sampling, beginning rejection sampling for an unnormalized target distribution and a tractable proposal distribution.

nodes.title: 11.1.2 Rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text concludes the transformation-based generation of Gaussian variables, deriving independent standard normals from uniform variables and extending this to multivariate Gaussians through Cholesky decomposition. Because transformation methods require tractable inverse integrals, it introduces rejection sampling as a broader approach: samples from an easy proposal distribution are accepted under an envelope defined by a scaled proposal, with acceptance controlled by the area ratio. A gamma-distribution example uses a shifted and scaled Cauchy proposal. It then introduces adaptive rejection sampling, in which tangent lines to the log density construct and iteratively refine an envelope for log-concave targets.

nodes.title: 11.1.3 Adaptive rejection sampling
nodes.summary: The text completes the discussion of rejection sampling by giving an optimized scaled-Cauchy envelope for a gamma target, then introduces adaptive rejection sampling for log-concave distributions. Tangent lines to the log density create a piecewise-exponential envelope that is refined whenever samples are rejected; derivative-free and Metropolis-extended variants are noted. It explains that rejection sampling suffers an exponential decline in acceptance rate with dimensionality, illustrated using Gaussian target and proposal distributions, making it unsuitable for most high-dimensional problems. The text then introduces importance sampling, which estimates expectations without directly sampling from the target: samples are drawn from an easier proposal distribution and weighted by the target-to-proposal density ratio, avoiding the severe inefficiency of uniform grids in high-dimensional spaces.

nodes.title: 11.1.4 Importance sampling
nodes.summary: The text introduces importance sampling as a way to estimate expectations under a difficult distribution by sampling from an easier proposal and applying importance weights. It explains grid-based inefficiency, ordinary and self-normalized estimators, unknown normalization constants, and the risks of poor proposal matching, including weight degeneracy, low effective sample size, missed high-mass regions, and undetectable large errors. It then describes uniform sampling and likelihood-weighted sampling for discrete graphical models, including their weighting rules and limitations, mentions adaptive self-importance sampling, and transitions to sampling-importance-resampling by highlighting the difficulty of selecting the rejection constant.

nodes.title: 11.1.5 Sampling-importance-resampling
nodes.summary: The text discusses limitations and graphical-model applications of importance sampling, including weight degeneracy, undetected bias, uniform sampling, likelihood weighting, and self-importance sampling. It then explains sampling-importance-resampling, its weighted resampling procedure, convergence to the target distribution, dependence on the proposal, and use of weights for moment estimation. Finally, it describes Monte Carlo EM, its MAP extension, and stochastic EM for mixture models.

nodes.title: 11.1.6 Sampling and the EM algorithm
nodes.summary: The text first notes that importance-sampling expectations can be estimated with weighted sample averages. It then explains Monte Carlo EM, in which samples from the latent-variable posterior approximate the EM E step, with a MAP extension obtained by adding the parameter prior; stochastic EM is described as the one-sample-per-step mixture-model case yielding hard assignments. For Bayesian inference, it presents data augmentation, alternating imputation and posterior steps to sample latent variables and update parameter posteriors when joint sampling is difficult. Finally, it motivates Markov chain Monte Carlo as a more powerful approach than rejection or importance sampling for high-dimensional distributions.

This section develops basic sampling methods from uniform random generation and transformation-based sampling to Gaussian generation via Box–Muller and Cholesky decompositions. It introduces rejection sampling and adaptive rejection sampling, including proposal-envelope construction, gamma and log-concave examples, and their poor high-dimensional scalability. It then presents importance sampling and its ordinary, self-normalized, graphical-model, likelihood-weighting, and adaptive forms, explaining weight degeneracy and proposal-mismatch risks. Sampling-importance-resampling is described as a weighted resampling alternative, and the section concludes with Monte Carlo, MAP, and stochastic EM, Bayesian data augmentation, and the motivation for MCMC in high-dimensional settings.

nodes.title: 11.2. Markov Chain Monte Carlo
11.2.1 Markov chains
nodes.summary: The text introduces the inefficiency of random-walk exploration, then develops Markov-chain foundations for MCMC: the Markov property, transition and marginal distributions, homogeneity, invariant distributions, detailed balance and reversibility, ergodicity, and construction of composite transitions through mixtures or successive base updates. It next presents Metropolis-Hastings for asymmetric proposals, gives its acceptance probability and detailed-balance proof, notes that normalization is unnecessary and symmetric proposals recover Metropolis, and begins examining how proposal variance affects performance. A figure illustrates accepted and rejected Metropolis moves when sampling a Gaussian.

nodes.title: 11.2.2 The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains how Markov transitions can be mixed or composed, including their invariance and detailed-balance properties, and notes the use of component-wise transitions. It then presents the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm for asymmetric proposals, gives its acceptance rule and detailed-balance proof, and discusses how Gaussian proposal scale affects acceptance, random-walk behavior, and convergence for anisotropic distributions. Finally, it introduces Gibbs sampling as a conditional-update MCMC method and a special case of Metropolis-Hastings.

This section introduces Bayesian data augmentation and then develops Markov chain Monte Carlo for sampling difficult, potentially high-dimensional posterior distributions. It explains the Metropolis method and its handling of proposals, rejection, dependence, convergence, and thinning; establishes the underlying theory of Markov chains, invariant distributions, detailed balance, reversibility, ergodicity, and composite transitions; generalizes the method to asymmetric proposals through Metropolis-Hastings; analyzes proposal scale and anisotropy; and concludes with Gibbs sampling as a conditional-update special case.

nodes.title: 11.3. Gibbs Sampling
Josiah Willard Gibbs
nodes.summary: Gibbs sampling generates samples by cycling through variables and drawing each from its full conditional distribution. The target distribution is invariant under these updates, but ergodicity, initialization, and autocorrelation must be considered. Gibbs sampling is equivalent to always-accepted Metropolis-Hastings updates. Correlated distributions can cause slow random-walk mixing, motivating over-relaxation and block updates. The method is especially useful in graphical models, where conditionals depend on Markov blankets and may be sampled using conjugacy or adaptive rejection sampling; replacing sampling with maximization yields ICM. The section also includes a biography of Josiah Willard Gibbs and introduces slice sampling as an adaptive alternative that augments the state with an auxiliary variable and samples under the distribution.

The section explains Gibbs sampling as a variable-by-variable MCMC method based on full conditional distributions, including its invariance, Metropolis–Hastings interpretation, requirements for ergodicity, initialization and autocorrelation considerations, and slow mixing for correlated variables. It discusses over-relaxation and block updates, applications to graphical models through Markov blankets and conjugate or adaptive-rejection conditional sampling, and the ICM maximization variant. It also provides biographical material on Josiah Willard Gibbs and introduces slice sampling as an adaptive auxiliary-variable method.

nodes.title: 11.4. Slice Sampling
nodes.summary: The text explains Gibbs sampling refinements, including Markov-blanket conditionals, adaptive rejection sampling, ICM, and blocking. It then presents slice sampling, which augments the target with an auxiliary variable and uses adaptive interval expansion and shrinkage to draw from horizontal slices, with a component-wise multivariate extension. Finally, it introduces hybrid Monte Carlo as a gradient-based alternative to random-walk Metropolis methods and begins its formulation through Hamiltonian dynamics and momentum variables.

nodes.title: 11.5. The Hybrid Monte Carlo Algorithm
11.5.1 Dynamical systems
William Hamilton
nodes.summary: The text develops the Hamiltonian foundations of hybrid Monte Carlo. It introduces position and momentum variables, potential and kinetic energy, and the Hamiltonian equations of motion. Hamiltonian trajectories conserve total energy and phase-space volume, making the distribution proportional to exp(-H) invariant, while momentum resampling is needed to achieve ergodic exploration. Because numerical integration is required, it presents the volume-preserving leapfrog scheme, its update sequence, and its discretization errors, which HMC subsequently corrects. The method alternates leapfrog dynamics with Gaussian momentum resampling and exploits gradient information for efficient high-dimensional sampling. A sidebar describes William Rowan Hamilton’s career, contributions to dynamics, and invention of quaternions.

This section develops Hamiltonian dynamics as the foundation of hybrid Monte Carlo: it represents target-distribution variables as positions with auxiliary momenta, defines the Hamiltonian and its equations of motion, and explains energy conservation and phase-space-volume preservation. It discusses momentum refreshment for ergodicity, numerical leapfrog integration and its errors, and the alternating integration–momentum-resampling procedure that enables efficient gradient-based sampling and is later corrected by Metropolis acceptance. A sidebar provides biographical context on William Rowan Hamilton and his work in dynamics and quaternions.

nodes.title: 11.5.2 Hybrid Monte Carlo
nodes.summary: The text explains Hybrid Monte Carlo as a Metropolis-corrected leapfrog method that removes discretization bias. It gives the acceptance rule and establishes detailed balance through random time direction, leapfrog reversibility, and exact phase-space volume preservation. It discusses periodic trajectories, the need to randomize step sizes for ergodicity, and the efficiency of HMC on Gaussian targets compared with random-walk Metropolis. It then introduces partition functions, their role in Bayesian model comparison, and importance sampling as a way to estimate ratios of partition functions.

The section develops Hybrid Monte Carlo from Hamiltonian dynamics, covering position–momentum representations, Hamiltonian conservation laws, volume preservation, momentum refreshment, leapfrog integration and its errors, and the alternating sampling procedure. It then explains the Metropolis correction, acceptance and detailed balance, trajectory periodicity, step-size randomization, and HMC's efficiency relative to random-walk methods. Historical context on Hamilton is included, followed by an introduction to partition functions, Bayesian model comparison, and importance sampling for estimating partition-function ratios.

nodes.title: 11.6. Estimating the Partition Function
nodes.summary: The text compares the efficiency of leapfrog-based hybrid Monte Carlo and ordinary Metropolis sampling for anisotropic Gaussian scales, then explains partition functions, their role in Bayesian model evidence, and importance-sampling estimators for partition-function ratios. It discusses proposal-matching requirements, Markov-chain-based importance distributions, and chaining through interpolating intermediate energy functions to estimate difficult normalization constants, including the use of one chain across stages. It concludes with exercises covering estimator properties, transformations and Gaussian sampling, rejection and adaptive rejection sampling, piecewise exponential sampling, and the second moment of a simple random walk.

nodes.title: 11.6 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sampling methods, covering Monte Carlo estimator moments, inverse-transform sampling, transformations to Cauchy and Gaussian distributions, Cholesky-based multivariate Gaussian generation, rejection and adaptive rejection sampling, piecewise exponential sampling, random-walk moments, Gibbs sampling and detailed balance, ergodicity, conditional distributions in a Gaussian–gamma model, over-relaxation, Hamiltonian dynamics, and Gaussian conditional distributions.

nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on Gibbs sampling, ergodicity, detailed balance, conditional distributions for a Gaussian model with unknown mean and precision, over-relaxation updates, equivalence of Hamiltonian and alternative sampling equations, and proving that a conditional distribution is Gaussian. It also describes Figures 11.15 and 11.16, illustrating a disconnected uniform distribution over two variables and a Gaussian observation model with priors on its mean and precision.
