nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on Gibbs sampling and related methods. It covers detailed balance, Gibbs-sampling ergodicity for a disconnected uniform distribution, derivation of Gaussian and gamma conditional distributions in a simple Bayesian Gaussian model, verification of the mean and variance of an over-relaxation update, equivalence between Hamiltonian formulations, and proof that a conditional distribution is Gaussian. Figures illustrate the disconnected joint distribution over z1 and z2 and the graphical model for x, μ, and τ.

nodes.title: 11.16 ( ) By making use of (11.56), (11.57), and (11.63), show that the conditional distribution p(r|z) is a Gaussian.
nodes.summary: The text presents two figures and six exercises on Gibbs and Hamiltonian sampling. It covers detailed balance, ergodicity for a disconnected uniform distribution, derivation of Gaussian and gamma conditional distributions in a Gaussian model, verification of the mean and variance of an over-relaxation update, equivalence between Hamiltonian and earlier update equations, and proof that a specified conditional distribution is Gaussian.

nodes.title: 11.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text transitions from a hybrid Monte Carlo detailed-balance exercise to an introduction to continuous latent-variable models and low-dimensional manifold structure. It explains digit-image and oil-flow examples, generative modeling with latent variables and noise, and the progression from linear-Gaussian models to probabilistic PCA, factor analysis, mixtures, Bayesian methods, independent component analysis, and nonlinear models. It then develops PCA, presenting its maximum-variance and minimum-error formulations, deriving principal components as covariance-matrix eigenvectors, describing the M-dimensional solution and computational costs, and beginning the orthonormal-basis derivation of the minimum-error representation.

This section develops Monte Carlo methods for approximate inference, beginning with direct sampling, expectation estimation, graphical-model sampling, rejection methods, and importance sampling. It then presents MCMC theory and algorithms—Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs, slice sampling, and hybrid Monte Carlo—covering correctness, convergence, dependence, efficiency, adaptive and blocked updates, Hamiltonian dynamics, and practical limitations. It also explains partition functions and their estimation for Bayesian model comparison, provides extensive exercises and illustrative figures on sampling theory and Gaussian models, and concludes by introducing latent-variable manifold models and the foundations of principal component analysis.

Appendix B completes the development of approximate inference by giving an explicit Gaussian variational solution and then covering variational model comparison, Bayesian Gaussian mixtures, linear and logistic regression, exponential-family and message-passing methods, local convex-duality bounds, and expectation propagation. It derives posterior and predictive distributions, lower bounds, evidence approximations, iterative and sequential algorithms, model-selection procedures, sparsity and label-switching effects, factorization principles, and relationships among variational Bayes, EM, belief propagation, ADF, and alpha-divergences. A broad set of exercises reinforces these derivations, asymptotic results, Gaussian and mixture models, regression, and EP. The material then transitions to sampling-based approximate inference, introducing Monte Carlo, rejection and importance sampling, MCMC algorithms, partition-function estimation, and latent-variable manifold methods.

nodes.title: Appendix C
12.1.2 Minimum-error formulation
nodes.summary: The text explains PCA as the selection of covariance-matrix eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues to maximize projected variance, including computational costs and efficient methods for finding only the leading components. It then derives an equivalent minimum-reconstruction-error formulation using a complete orthonormal basis: optimal coefficients give orthogonal projections, the subspace passes through the data mean, and the minimum distortion is the sum of the omitted eigenvalues. A two-dimensional example illustrates why the largest-variance direction is selected, followed by the general solution, the special case M=D, and a comparison with canonical correlation analysis. It concludes by introducing PCA-based compression of handwritten-digit data.

nodes.title: 12.1.3 Applications of peA
nodes.summary: The text completes the mathematical justification of PCA, showing that covariance eigenvectors define stationary directions of the projection-distortion objective, that the M largest-eigenvalue directions form the optimal principal subspace, and that discarded eigenvalues determine the minimum distortion. It notes the no-reduction case M=D and relates PCA to CCA. Applications include digit-image compression and reconstruction, standardization and whitening for preprocessing, comparison with supervised Fisher discriminants, and two-dimensional visualization. The final section addresses high-dimensional settings with fewer samples than dimensions, explaining the resulting zero eigenvalues, the limit of N−1 useful components, and the computational difficulty of direct eigendecomposition.

nodes.title: 12.1.4 peA for high-dimensional data
nodes.summary: The text compares unsupervised PCA with label-aware Fisher discriminant analysis, illustrates PCA projections for airflow data, and explains an efficient approach to PCA when dimensionality exceeds the number of observations. By using the centered data matrix and solving an N×N rather than D×D eigenproblem, computational cost is reduced and the original eigenvectors can be reconstructed with proper normalization. It then introduces probabilistic PCA as a maximum-likelihood latent-variable formulation that restricts Gaussian parameters while preserving dominant data correlations.

nodes.title: 12.2. Probabilistic peA
12.2.1 Maximum likelihood peA
nodes.summary: The text develops maximum-likelihood probabilistic PCA. It derives the likelihood and shows that the mean is the sample mean, while the optimal loading matrix spans the principal eigenvectors of the sample covariance, scaled by eigenvalue-minus-noise terms and subject to arbitrary latent-space rotations. The optimal isotropic noise is the average discarded eigenvalue, yielding exact variance along retained principal directions and an averaged variance elsewhere. It discusses rotational non-identifiability, the M = D reduction to a full Gaussian, posterior latent projections and their zero-noise PCA limit, and PPCA’s controlled parameter complexity relative to full and diagonal covariance models. Finally, it introduces EM estimation for PPCA, emphasizing its computational, missing-data, and factor-analysis advantages.

nodes.title: 12.2.2 EM algorithm for peA
nodes.summary: The text explains PPCA’s parameter efficiency and limiting cases, derives its effective covariance degrees of freedom, and develops an EM algorithm using latent posterior sufficient statistics to update W and σ². It discusses why EM can outperform covariance-based PCA in high-dimensional or large-scale settings, including online implementation, missing-data handling, and the zero-noise limit that recovers standard PCA. A spring-and-rod analogy illustrates the E and M steps, while a figure demonstrates visualization with missing flow-data values. Finally, it introduces Bayesian PCA and eigenvalue-spectrum heuristics for selecting the latent dimensionality.

nodes.title: 12.2.3 Bayesian peA
nodes.summary: The text explains EM for probabilistic PCA, including its spring-and-rod interpretation and figures showing convergence and robustness to missing-data imputation. It then introduces Bayesian PCA for selecting latent dimensionality, contrasting eigenvalue inspection and cross-validation with an ARD-based Bayesian method that assigns separate Gaussian-prior precisions to columns of W, prunes irrelevant directions, and estimates parameters through marginal-likelihood maximization with a Laplace approximation interleaved with EM. It describes the resulting update behavior, limiting cases, computational trade-offs, comparisons with standard PCA, and a Gibbs-sampling example showing multiple posterior modes. Fully Bayesian extensions and related dimensionality-selection references are noted, followed by an introduction to factor analysis as a closely related linear-Gaussian model.

nodes.title: 12.2.4 Factor analysis
nodes.summary: The text presents Bayesian PCA with Laplace-based hyperparameter re-estimation, EM updates, effective-dimensionality selection, Gibbs-sampling behavior, and references to fully Bayesian extensions. It then defines factor analysis as probabilistic PCA with diagonal rather than isotropic noise, explains loadings, uniquenesses, covariance structure, rotational non-identifiability, its historical relationship to PCA, marginal distribution, maximum-likelihood EM equations, computational advantages, Bayesian treatment, and behavior under data rescaling. Finally, it introduces kernel PCA as a nonlinear kernelized form of PCA, beginning with centered data, the covariance eigenproblem, and a feature-space mapping.

The section first reviews a dual computational formulation of PCA and then develops probabilistic PCA as a linear-Gaussian latent-variable model. It covers the model’s generative and marginal distributions, practical advantages, maximum-likelihood solution and its relation to ordinary PCA, parameter identifiability and complexity, posterior projections, and EM estimation, including computational efficiency, online learning, missing data, and visualization. It then treats Bayesian PCA and automatic dimensionality selection through ARD, Laplace-based evidence optimization, EM and Gibbs sampling, before introducing factor analysis with diagonal noise and its estimation, identifiability, Bayesian extensions, and scaling behavior. The section concludes by introducing kernel PCA as a nonlinear feature-space generalization.

nodes.title: 12.3. Kernel peA
nodes.summary: The text concludes the discussion of factor analysis by noting efficient diagonal-noise M-step equations, Bayesian extensions, and the differing transformation invariances of PCA/probabilistic PCA and factor analysis. It then develops kernel PCA by mapping data implicitly into a feature space, reformulating the covariance eigenproblem entirely through an N × N kernel Gram matrix, specifying eigenvector normalization and kernel-based projections, and explaining dimensionality limits. It derives kernel-matrix centering for nonzero feature-space means, notes recovery of ordinary PCA with a linear kernel, illustrates the method with a Gaussian-kernel synthetic clustering example, and discusses its computational cost and the difficulty of obtaining original-space pre-images from feature-space projections.

nodes.title: 12.4. Nonlinear Latent Variable Models
12.4.1 Independent component analysis
nodes.summary: The text introduces nonlinear and non-Gaussian latent-variable models and focuses on independent component analysis, where observed variables are linear mixtures of statistically independent, non-Gaussian latent variables. It explains ICA through blind speech-source separation, discusses its deterministic equal-dimensional generative model and likelihood optimization, and shows why Gaussian latent models cannot identify independent components because of rotational indeterminacy and the insufficiency of zero correlation for independence. A heavy-tailed 1/cosh latent density is given, followed by discussion of information-maximization ICA and independent factor analysis, which extends ICA with unequal dimensions, noise, mixture-of-Gaussian latent distributions, EM learning, and variational reconstruction. The section closes by noting the broad ICA literature and introducing autoassociative neural networks.

nodes.title: 12.4.2 Autoassociative neural networks
outputs
nodes.summary: The text explains autoassociative neural networks for dimensionality reduction. Two-layer networks trained to reconstruct their inputs reproduce linear PCA even with nonlinear hidden units, whereas deeper networks with nonlinear layers can learn nonlinear latent manifolds, at the cost of difficult nonconvex optimization, possible local minima, and a required choice of latent dimension. It then discusses modeling nonlinear manifolds through local PCA or mixtures of probabilistic PCA/factor-analysis models, including EM, Bayesian variational inference, parameter-sharing variants, and hierarchical visualization models. Finally, it introduces principal curves as a single nonlinear generalization of PCA for representing one-dimensional manifolds and projecting data onto them.

The section first explains why ICA requires non-Gaussian latent variables: Gaussian linear latent models are rotationally ambiguous, and decorrelation does not ensure independence. It describes heavy-tailed latent distributions and probabilistic ICA extensions such as independent factor analysis, including noisy observations, flexible mixture models, EM, and variational inference. It then presents autoassociative neural networks for dimensionality reduction, showing that shallow reconstruction networks recover PCA whereas deeper nonlinear networks learn nonlinear manifolds but introduce nonconvex optimization and latent-dimension-selection problems. It also covers local and mixture-based probabilistic PCA or factor-analysis approaches, EM and Bayesian variational inference, parameter sharing, hierarchical visualization models, and principal curves as a one-dimensional nonlinear analogue of PCA.

nodes.title: 12.4.3 Modelling nonlinear manifolds
nodes.summary: The text surveys nonlinear latent-variable and manifold-learning methods, beginning with nonlinear PCA networks and their optimization limitations, then discussing piecewise-linear mixtures of PCA, probabilistic mixtures and Bayesian variants, principal curves and surfaces, MDS, LLE, and Isomap. It covers latent trait models for discrete observations, density networks using neural transformations and Monte Carlo integration, and GTM as an efficient probabilistic nonlinear manifold model, contrasting it with SOMs and describing GTM extensions and geometric diagnostics. The section concludes with exercises on PCA eigenvector proofs, Gaussian transformations and probabilistic PCA derivations, posterior behavior, and optimal reconstruction.

This section surveys nonlinear latent-variable and manifold models, beginning with ICA and the necessity of non-Gaussianity for identifying independent components, then extending the framework through noisy, flexible probabilistic models learned by likelihood, EM, or variational methods. It covers autoassociative networks, PCA and probabilistic factor-analysis mixtures, nonlinear dimensionality reduction, principal curves and surfaces, manifold-learning algorithms such as MDS, LLE, and Isomap, latent trait and density-network models, and GTM with its extensions and comparison to SOMs. It also addresses optimization, identifiability, visualization, geometric diagnostics, and exercises involving PCA and probabilistic modeling.

nodes.title: 12.3 (*) Verify that the eigenvectors defined by (12.30) are normalized to unit length, assuming that the eigenvectors Vi have unit length.
nodes.summary: This text introduces a set of exercises on probabilistic PCA and related Gaussian transformations. It covers eigenvector normalization and equivalent eigenvector solutions; invariance of the model under general Gaussian latent distributions; affine transformations of Gaussian variables; graphical-model independence structure; derivations of the marginal and posterior distributions; maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the data mean; the zero-noise connection between probabilistic PCA and conventional PCA; the effect of positive noise on posterior projections; and the least-squares optimal reconstruction formula.

nodes.title: 12.12 (* *) For (Y2 > 0 show that the posterior mean in the probabilistic PCA model is shifted towards the origin relative to the orthogonal projection.
nodes.summary: This text introduces exercises on probabilistic PCA and related Gaussian transformations. It covers eigenvector normalization, equivalence of general and standard latent Gaussian parameterizations, affine transformations of Gaussian variables and dimensionality cases, graphical-model independence structure, derivation of the probabilistic PCA marginal and posterior distributions, maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the mean, limiting behavior toward conventional PCA projections, shrinkage toward the origin for nonzero noise, and the least-squares optimal reconstruction.

nodes.title: 12.13 (* *) Show that the optimal reconstruction of a data point under probabilistic PCA, according to the least squares projection cost of conventional PCA, is given by
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on probabilistic PCA and factor analysis. It covers eigenvector normalization and equivalent solutions; invariance of probabilistic PCA under general Gaussian latent priors; affine transformations of Gaussian variables; graphical-model independence structure; derivation of probabilistic PCA marginal and posterior distributions; maximum-likelihood estimation and uniqueness of the mean; zero- and nonzero-noise behavior of posterior projections; optimal reconstruction; covariance parameter counting; EM update derivations, including missing-data EM; the connection between least-squares linear reconstruction and PCA E- and M-steps; and factor-analysis parameter counting, rotational invariance, mean optimization, and EM posterior updates.

nodes.title: 12.19 (**) IIiI!I Show that the factor analysis model described in Section 12.2.4 is invariant under rotations of the latent space coordinates.
nodes.summary: The exercises develop probabilistic PCA, factor analysis, mixtures, transformations, and kernel PCA. They address parameter counting, EM derivations with complete and missing data, least-squares interpretations of PCA, factor-analysis identifiability and maximum-likelihood updates, graphical models for PCA mixtures, the EM algorithm for Student's t-distributions, covariance and parameter transformations under linear changes of data coordinates, equivalence of kernel-PCA formulations and recovery of ordinary PCA, nonlinear change-of-variable constructions for probability densities, and the distinction between independence and uncorrelatedness.

nodes.title: 13 Sequential Data
13.1. Markov Models
nodes.summary: The text develops Markov and state space models for sequential data. It contrasts i.i.d. modeling with first- and higher-order Markov chains, gives their factorizations and conditional-independence properties, and explains stationarity, parameter growth, autoregressive models, and neural-network alternatives. It then introduces latent Markov states, whose observation model forms a state space model in which observations can depend on the entire history despite the latent chain being first-order Markov. The two main cases are hidden Markov models with discrete latent states and linear dynamical systems with Gaussian variables. HMMs are interpreted as temporally dependent mixture models, with applications across speech, language, handwriting, and biological sequences, and their latent transitions are specified by a row-normalized transition matrix.

nodes.title: 13.2. Hidden Markov Models
13.2.1 Maximum likelihood for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text explains HMMs’ ability to model local temporal warping, illustrated with handwritten digits and speech, while noting their strong sensitivity to sequence direction. It then develops maximum-likelihood learning for HMMs: direct marginalization over latent state paths is exponentially costly and direct optimization is not closed-form, so EM is used. The E-step computes single-state and adjacent-state posterior marginals, gamma and xi, and forms the expected complete-data log likelihood. The M-step updates initial and transition probabilities by normalized expected counts and estimates emission parameters through weighted likelihood maximization, with explicit Gaussian and multinomial formulas and analogous Bernoulli treatment. It discusses initialization, persistence of zero probabilities, and left-to-right models, and introduces the forward-backward/Baum-Welch algorithm as the efficient method for obtaining the required posterior quantities.

nodes.title: 13.2.2 The forward-backward algorithm
nodes.summary: The text completes the EM treatment of hidden Markov models by presenting emission-specific M-step updates for Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli observations, discussing parameter initialization, and deriving the forward-backward algorithm for the E step. It uses HMM conditional independences and d-separation to define and recursively compute forward and backward messages, obtain state and transition posteriors, evaluate the likelihood efficiently, and explain the O(K²N) cost. It then summarizes complete EM training, initialization and data-length considerations, derives fixed-memory next-observation prediction, and discusses regularized and fully Bayesian extensions. Finally, it recasts the HMM as a factor graph and introduces the equivalent sum-product derivation using initial and transition-emission factors.

nodes.title: 13.2.3 The sum-product algorithm for the HMM
nodes.summary: The text explains how HMM inference and learning extend beyond maximum likelihood, including regularized, Bayesian, and variational approaches. It derives the forward-backward alpha-beta recursions through the sum-product algorithm on a simplified factor graph, showing how forward and backward messages produce hidden-state marginals and related pairwise quantities. It then addresses numerical underflow in long sequences, motivating normalized forward and backward variables and conditional-likelihood scaling factors.

nodes.title: 13.2.4 Scaling factors
nodes.summary: The text connects HMM forward-backward inference with sum-product message passing, showing that beta messages and alpha-beta products yield the state and pairwise marginals. It explains numerical underflow in unscaled forward-backward recursions and introduces normalization-based scaling factors, scaled alpha and beta recursions, likelihood evaluation, and stable marginal formulas. It also presents the alternative alpha-gamma formulation. Finally, it introduces the Viterbi max-sum algorithm for finding the globally most probable hidden-state sequence, contrasts it with independently maximizing state marginals, and notes its logarithmic, linear-time dynamic-programming implementation.

nodes.title: 13.2.5 The Viterbi algorithm
nodes.summary: The text contrasts the α–γ and α–β forward-backward formulations, then presents the Viterbi max-sum algorithm for finding the globally most probable HMM state sequence rather than independently most probable states. It gives the log-domain message recursion, initialization, dynamic-programming interpretation, computational advantage, and predecessor backtracking procedure. It concludes by introducing HMM extensions, especially discriminative rather than maximum-likelihood training for sequence classification, defining the class-posterior cross-entropy objective and its Bayes-based form.

nodes.title: 13.2.6 Extensions of the hidden Markov model
nodes.summary: The text explains the dynamic-programming intuition behind Viterbi decoding and surveys major HMM extensions. It covers discriminative training for sequence classification, explicit state-duration modelling, autoregressive and input-output HMMs, and factorial HMMs, emphasizing their probabilistic structures, d-separation properties, EM or forward-backward training, computational costs, and variational or sampling-based solutions for intractable inference. It concludes by motivating linear dynamical systems through noisy measurement of a changing quantity, contrasting global averages, sliding windows, and weighted averages for balancing noise reduction and temporal responsiveness.

This section develops hidden Markov models as discrete-state state-space and temporally dependent mixture models, defining their initial and transition probabilities, emission distributions, joint probability, graphical and trellis representations, applications, and relation to ordinary mixture models. It presents maximum-likelihood estimation through EM, including posterior sufficient statistics and parameter updates for common emission families, then derives forward-backward and sum-product algorithms for efficient likelihood and posterior computation. Numerical scaling methods address underflow, while fixed-memory prediction and regularized, Bayesian, and variational approaches extend inference and learning. The Viterbi algorithm is introduced for globally optimal state-sequence decoding. The section concludes with discriminative training and structural HMM extensions such as duration, autoregressive, input-output, and factorial models, and motivates linear dynamical systems for noisy time-varying measurements.

nodes.title: 13.3. Linear Dynamical Systems
13.3.1 Inference in LDS
nodes.summary: The text develops inference for linear dynamical systems using Gaussian sum-product message passing. It derives the Kalman filter forward recursions for predicted and updated state means, covariances, Kalman gains, normalization constants, initial conditions, and likelihood evaluation, and interprets filtering as repeated prediction and observation-based correction. It discusses limiting noise regimes and tracking applications. It then derives backward smoothing recursions for posteriors conditioned on all observations, explains their role in parameter learning, and gives the Gaussian pairwise smoothed marginals and cross-covariances needed by EM.

nodes.title: 13.3.2 Learning in LDS
nodes.summary: The text derives EM-based maximum-likelihood parameter learning for linear dynamical systems, including the required posterior expectations, complete-data objective, and closed-form updates for the initial distribution, transition dynamics, and observation model. It briefly mentions MAP and Bayesian extensions, then surveys LDS extensions, explaining the tractability of mixture initial states, the exponential complexity of mixture emissions, approximate and sampling-based inference for non-Gaussian models, the extended Kalman filter, and switching state-space and switching hidden Markov models.

nodes.title: 13.3.3 Extensions of LDS
nodes.summary: The text discusses LDS parameter learning through maximum likelihood, MAP estimation with priors, and possible fully Bayesian approximations. It then surveys LDS extensions: mixture initial distributions remain tractable, whereas mixture emissions cause exponential posterior growth. Nonlinear or non-Gaussian models generally require deterministic approximations, sampling, or extended Kalman filtering. Finally, it describes switching state space models, their intractable exact inference and variational solution, and the related switching hidden Markov model.

nodes.title: 13.3.4 Particle filters
nodes.summary: The text develops particle filtering for nonlinear or non-Gaussian dynamical systems. It derives a weighted-particle approximation to p(z_n|X_n) using samples from the predictive distribution and likelihood-based normalized weights, then derives the next-step predictive distribution as a mixture over transition models. The algorithm repeatedly samples particles from this mixture and reweights them using the new observation. The relevant conditional independences are justified by d-separation, and alternative names for the method are listed. The section concludes with an exercise on verifying Markov-model independences using d-separation.

This section introduces linear dynamical systems as linear-Gaussian state-space models for tracking changing latent quantities from noisy sequential data. It defines their Markov transition, observation, and initial distributions; explains their relationship to HMMs and continuous latent-variable models; and shows why Gaussian closure enables efficient sum-product inference. It develops Kalman filtering and Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing, including likelihoods and the posterior moments required for learning, then derives EM parameter updates and discusses MAP and Bayesian alternatives. The section surveys mixture, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, switching, and extended-Kalman-filter variants, and concludes with particle filtering based on weighted predictive samples, observation reweighting, and d-separation.

nodes.title: 13.1 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text derives the particle filter’s predictive distribution as a weighted mixture of state-transition distributions using Bayes’ theorem and d-separation-based conditional independences. It explains sampling from this mixture and summarizes particle filtering as propagating weighted particles and then reweighting them with the next observation, with an illustration and alternative names for the method. The exercises cover verifying first- and second-order Markov conditional independences by d-separation and probability rules, proving that the observed state-space process lacks finite-order Markov structure, and describing maximum-likelihood learning of parametric emission-model parameters.

nodes.title: 13.4 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents a schematic particle-filter operation and then lists exercises on Markov and second-order Markov conditional independencies, d-separation in state-space and hidden Markov models, maximum-likelihood and EM learning for parametric and Gaussian or discrete emissions, constrained updates for initial and transition probabilities, persistence of zero parameters, derivation of HMM posterior quantities via factor graphs and sum-product, and EM training across multiple independent sequences.

nodes.title: 13.8 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on EM training and probabilistic structure in hidden Markov models. It covers deriving and verifying M-step updates for initial, transition, Gaussian-emission, multinomial-emission, and Bernoulli-emission parameters; proving that zero initial probabilities remain zero; verifying HMM conditional independencies through d-separation and probability rules; deriving pairwise latent-state posteriors using factor-graph sum-product messages; and extending EM inference and parameter re-estimation to multiple independent observation sequences.

nodes.title: 13.9 ( ) www
nodes.summary: Exercises 13.5–13.16 develop and verify HMM inference and learning results. They derive EM updates for initial, transition, Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli emission parameters; examine preservation of zero parameters; verify HMM conditional independences both graphically and probabilistically; derive pairwise latent-state posteriors and scaled marginal formulas; extend EM to multiple independent sequences; establish the equivalence of factor-graph alpha and beta messages with standard forward-backward recursions; and derive the Viterbi forward recursion from the joint distribution.

nodes.title: 13.13 ( ) www
nodes.summary: This section presents multi-sequence Baum–Welch parameter re-estimation formulas, including the responsibility-weighted Gaussian mean update, followed by exercises on factor-graph interpretations of HMM alpha and beta messages, rescaled HMM marginals, the Viterbi recursion, input-output HMM factorization and inference, Gaussian posterior maximization in linear dynamical systems, derivations of Kalman filter and smoother identities, affine-offset extensions of linear-Gaussian models through state augmentation, and the reduction of Kalman filtering for independent observations to the maximum-likelihood estimate of a single Gaussian mean.

nodes.title: 13.17 ( ) www
nodes.summary: This excerpt lists exercises on sequential data and linear dynamical systems. It covers identifying the initial condition of a recursion, expressing an input-output hidden Markov model as a tree-structured factor graph, deriving its forward-backward algorithm, proving equivalence between marginal posterior maximization and most-probable latent sequences in Gaussian systems, deriving several Kalman-filter and smoother identities using Gaussian and matrix results, extending the model to include constant offsets through state and matrix augmentation, and showing that the Kalman filter reduces to the maximum-likelihood estimator of a Gaussian mean for independent observations. The final exercise is only partially included.

nodes.title: 13.19 ( ) www
nodes.summary: The text presents exercises on sequential-data models, covering initialization and factor-graph formulations of input-output hidden Markov models, forward-backward recursions, Gaussian properties of latent-state posteriors, derivations of Kalman filtering and smoothing equations using matrix identities, affine extensions of linear dynamical systems, connections between Kalman filtering, independent Gaussian maximum likelihood, and probabilistic PCA, limiting cases with noiseless observations or constant states, pairwise posterior covariances, and verification of EM M-step updates for initial, transition, and emission parameters.

This section develops probabilistic models and inference methods for dependent sequential data, beginning with Markov and state-space models and progressing to hidden Markov models, linear dynamical systems, and particle filters. It covers model factorizations, conditional independence, stationarity, prediction, applications, parameter learning by maximum likelihood and EM, Bayesian and variational alternatives, forward-backward, sum-product, Viterbi, Kalman filtering and smoothing, numerical scaling, and particle-based inference. It also surveys major model extensions and provides exercises on conditional-independence proofs, factor-graph algorithms, HMM and LDS parameter updates, multi-sequence learning, Gaussian identities, affine and input-output models, and connections to Gaussian maximum likelihood and probabilistic PCA.

nodes.title: 14 Combining Models
14.1. Bayesian Model Averaging
nodes.summary: The text introduces model combination, in which input-dependent selection or weighting lets different models handle different regions or observations. It discusses hard selection through decision trees and soft probabilistic mixtures of experts, including their mathematical formulation and relation to mixture density networks. It distinguishes model combination from Bayesian model averaging: mixture models may assign different components to different data points, while Bayesian model averaging assumes one alternative model generated the entire dataset and updates uncertainty over that model. The distinction extends to predictive and conditional distributions. Finally, it introduces committees, which average predictions from several models, motivated by the bias-variance decomposition of prediction error.

nodes.title: 14.2. Committees
nodes.summary: The text distinguishes model combination from Bayesian model averaging and explains their effects on latent component assignments, whole-data model uncertainty, predictive densities, and conditional distributions. It then introduces committees, showing how averaging models can reduce variance and improve predictions, especially through bootstrap aggregation (bagging), and derives the committee error reduction under zero-mean, uncorrelated errors while noting the practical impact of correlated errors. Finally, it introduces boosting and AdaBoost, which sequentially train weighted weak classifiers, emphasize previously misclassified data, and combine the classifiers through weighted voting.

nodes.title: 14.3. Boosting
14.3.1 Minimizing exponential error
nodes.summary: This passage completes the AdaBoost description by explaining final prediction, adaptive data weighting, error-based learner coefficients, and the decision-stump illustration. It then derives AdaBoost as sequential minimization of an exponential loss: fixing earlier learners, the new learner minimizes weighted classification error, its coefficient is determined by weighted error, and the resulting update emphasizes misclassified examples. The passage also explains the ensemble decision rule and analyzes the exponential loss at the population level, showing that its optimal real-valued function is one-half the log posterior odds.

nodes.title: 14.3.2 Error functions for boosting
nodes.summary: The text completes the derivation of AdaBoost’s objective, coefficient selection, weight updates, and final sign-based prediction rule. It explains exponential loss as an approximation to log odds, compares it with cross-entropy and other error functions, and discusses its computational advantage, lack of probabilistic and multiclass interpretations, sensitivity to outliers, and extensions to multiclass and regression boosting. It then introduces tree-based models, including CART and related algorithms, as recursive binary partitions of input space with a simple model assigned to each axis-aligned region.

The section motivates boosting as a more effective alternative to simple model averaging and presents AdaBoost, which sequentially trains weak classifiers on adaptively reweighted data and combines them using error-based coefficients. It gives the algorithm, its exponential-loss derivation, final decision rule, and log-odds interpretation, then discusses exponential loss relative to other objectives, its computational and statistical limitations, extensions to multiclass classification and regression, and the use of recursive tree-based models such as CART as base learners.

nodes.title: 14.4. Tree-based Models
nodes.summary: The text first contrasts squared and absolute error, noting the robustness of absolute deviation to outliers and mislabeled data. It then explains CART tree-based models as interpretable recursive, axis-aligned partitions in which each leaf provides a simple prediction. It covers regression learning via regional averages and greedy split selection, followed by large-tree growth and complexity-penalized pruning chosen through cross-validation. For classification, it presents cross-entropy and Gini criteria for growth and misclassification rate for pruning. Finally, it discusses tree instability, inefficient axis-aligned and hard splits, and discontinuous regression outputs, motivating probabilistic soft-split alternatives such as hierarchical mixtures of experts and conditional mixtures of regression models.

nodes.title: 14.5. Conditional Mixture Models
14.5.1 Mixtures of linear regression models
nodes.summary: The text introduces conditional mixture models and explains mixtures of linear regressions in detail. It defines the Gaussian mixture of regression components, derives its latent-variable formulation and complete-data likelihood, and presents the EM algorithm: responsibilities are computed in the E step, while mixing coefficients, regression weights, and shared noise precision are updated in the M step. The regression updates are responsibility-weighted least-squares solutions. A two-line example demonstrates improved modeling of bimodal data over a single regression, while noting the limitation of input-independent mixture weights and motivating mixture density networks and hierarchical mixtures of experts. The section then introduces mixtures of logistic regression models, gives their conditional distribution and parameters, and begins the corresponding likelihood formulation.

nodes.title: 14.5.2 Mixtures of logistic models
nodes.summary: The text presents EM-based mixtures of linear and logistic regression models. It illustrates how a two-component linear mixture can model multimodal predictive distributions and outperform a single linear model. For mixtures of logistic regressions, it derives the likelihood, latent-variable complete likelihood, E-step responsibilities, expected log likelihood, and M-step updates: mixing proportions are averaged responsibilities, while component weights are independently fitted by IRLS as weighted logistic regressions. The approach extends to multiclass softmax mixtures. It then introduces mixtures of experts, in which input-dependent gating functions select among component experts so that different models can specialize in different regions of input space.

nodes.title: 14.5.3 Mixtures of experts
nodes.summary: The text completes the EM treatment of mixtures of logistic regression models, deriving the mixing-coefficient update, component-wise decoupling, gradient and Hessian, and IRLS-based weighted logistic-regression updates, with an illustrative classification example and mention of softmax extensions. It then introduces mixtures of experts with input-dependent gating functions, explains linear and hierarchical versions, their EM/IRLS training, relation to decision trees and mixture density networks, and their comparative advantages. The exercises cover Bayesian predictive marginalization and model averaging, committee-error derivations and Jensen inequalities, convex-error generalization, and conditions ensuring that unequally weighted committee predictions lie within the members’ prediction range.

This section motivates conditional mixture models as flexible probabilistic alternatives to unstable, hard, axis-aligned decision trees. It develops Gaussian mixtures of linear regressions and mixtures of logistic or softmax regressions using latent variables and EM, with responsibility-weighted least-squares or IRLS updates, and illustrates their ability to model multimodal regression and classification behavior. It then introduces mixtures of experts, whose input-dependent gating functions allow specialized linear or hierarchical experts, relating them to decision trees and mixture density networks. The section concludes with exercises on Bayesian prediction, committee model averaging, error bounds, Jensen inequalities, and prediction-range properties.

It then presents exercises on marginalizing model indices and latent variables in predictive distributions, distinguishing Bayesian model averaging from within-model latent variables, deriving committee-error relations, proving that a committee's expected error is no greater than the average member error via Jensen's inequality, extending the result to arbitrary convex error functions, and establishing that bounded weighted committee predictions require nonnegative weights summing to one.

It then presents exercises on marginalizing model indices and latent variables in predictive distributions and distinguishing Bayesian model averaging from within-model latent variables; deriving and proving committee-model error inequalities using Jensen’s inequality, including their extension to arbitrary convex losses; and establishing that bounded weighted committee predictions require nonnegative weights summing to one.

The exercises also extend, verify, and derive EM-based mixture-of-linear-regression results for vector targets, complete-data likelihoods, and mixing coefficients, and analyze the conditional-mean prediction and its limitations for multimodal mixtures.

This section surveys methods for improving classification and regression by combining models. It distinguishes input-dependent mixtures and mixtures of experts from Bayesian model averaging, develops committee averaging and bagging as variance-reduction methods, and presents boosting and AdaBoost with their loss-based derivations, interpretations, limitations, and extensions. It then covers CART regression and classification trees, their impurity criteria, pruning, instability, and shortcomings, motivating soft probabilistic conditional mixtures. Gaussian mixtures of linear regressions, logistic and softmax mixtures, EM estimation, and hierarchical mixtures of experts are developed for flexible multimodal prediction and classification, with comparisons to mixture density networks and analyses of hierarchical flattening. Exercises reinforce Bayesian marginalization, committee-error inequalities, convex-loss results, boosting, tree criteria, and EM-based mixture models, including vector targets and multimodal conditional predictions.

Appendix C covers dimensionality reduction and latent-variable modeling in depth, from conventional PCA and its variance, reconstruction, computational, preprocessing, visualization, and high-dimensional formulations to probabilistic PCA, factor analysis, Bayesian dimensionality selection, kernel PCA, and nonlinear manifold and latent-variable methods. It includes mathematical derivations, identifiability, invariances, EM, Bayesian and variational inference, missing data, visualization, and extensive exercises. The appendix then develops sequential probabilistic models—including Markov and state-space models, HMMs, LDSs, Kalman methods, and particle filters—and concludes with methods for combining predictive models, including averaging, bagging, boosting, decision trees, mixtures of regressions and classifiers, and hierarchical mixtures of experts.

structure.summary: The section surveys the foundations and broad methodology of probabilistic pattern recognition and machine learning. It progresses from probability distributions, Gaussian models, Bayesian inference, decision and information theory, and basic curve fitting to regression, classification, neural and kernel methods, Gaussian processes, graphical models, mixtures, EM, variational and sampling-based inference. It also develops dimensionality reduction, latent-variable and nonlinear manifold models, sequential probabilistic models, and ensemble and hierarchical predictive methods, while addressing estimation, uncertainty, optimization, model selection, computation, sparsity, missing data, and identifiability. Extensive exercises, examples, figures, biographies, references, and calculus-of-variations and Lagrange-multiplier appendices support the material.

structure.title: Appendix A. Data Sets

nodes.title: Handwritten Digits
nodes.summary: The appendix introduces the book's example data sets and directs readers to the book website for data files and formats. It describes MNIST handwritten digits, including their NIST origins, train/test sizes, collection and preprocessing methods, sample figure, and representative classification error rates. It also introduces the synthetic Oil Flow data set, explaining dual-energy gamma densitometry, why two energy measurements are needed to infer oil, water, and gas proportions, and how low flow produces stratified phase separation in the pipeline.

nodes.title: Oil Flow
nodes.summary: The text introduces a figure of 100 random MNIST digits, then describes the Oil Flow synthetic data set, which simulates dual-energy gamma densitometry for estimating oil, water, and gas fractions and their stratified, annular, or homogeneous flow configuration. It explains the measurement setup, 12-dimensional observations from six beams, tomographic interpretation, Poisson photon noise, data-generation procedure, labels and train/validation/test sizes, and the distinct linear, nonlinear, segmented, and intersecting manifold structures useful for prediction and visualization. It also presents the Old Faithful data set of 272 eruptions, recording duration and time to the next eruption, where duration helps predict the waiting time.

nodes.title: Old Faithful
nodes.summary: The text describes the manifold structure of oil-and-water measurement data under homogeneous, annular, and laminar phase configurations, including noise effects, nonlinearities, discontinuities, segmentation, and intersections. It then introduces the 272-observation Old Faithful data set of eruption duration and subsequent waiting time, noting the predictive relationship between them. Finally, it presents two recurring synthetic data sets: a noisy sinusoidal regression problem and a two-class Gaussian-mixture classification problem with analytically accessible posterior probabilities and optimal decision boundary.

nodes.title: Synthetic Data
nodes.summary: The text presents an Old Faithful eruption-duration plot and describes two synthetic data sets used throughout the book: a noisy sinusoidal regression set and a two-class Gaussian-based classification set. It explains their generation, the visualizations in Figures A.6 and A.7, and how known distributions allow the true conditional or posterior probabilities and the optimal classification boundary to be plotted.

structure.summary: This appendix introduces the data sets used throughout the book: MNIST handwritten digits; the synthetic Oil Flow measurements, their physical basis, noise, labels, sample sizes, and manifold structures; the Old Faithful eruption-duration and waiting-time observations; and recurring synthetic regression and classification examples. It also describes the relevant visualizations, data-generation procedures, predictive relationships, and analytically known probabilities and optimal decision boundaries, while directing readers to the book website for data files and formats.

structure.title: Appendix B. Probability Distributions

nodes.title: Bernoulli
nodes.summary: The appendix introduces key statistics of common exponential-family distributions and presents the Bernoulli distribution for a binary variable, including its parameterization, probability mass function, expectation, variance, mode, entropy, relationship to the binomial distribution, and beta conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Beta
nodes.summary: The text introduces beta and binomial probability distributions. It gives the beta distribution's domain, parameter constraints, density, moments, mode, conjugacy to the Bernoulli distribution, interpretation of its parameters, boundary behavior, uniform special case, and relation to the Dirichlet distribution. It then defines the binomial distribution for counts of successes in Bernoulli trials, providing its probability mass function, combinatorial coefficient, moments, mode, factorial definition, and its Bernoulli and Gaussian approximations, while noting that the beta distribution is its conjugate prior.

nodes.title: Binomial
nodes.summary: The text introduces the beta, binomial, and Dirichlet probability distributions, giving their domains, parameter constraints, probability or density formulas, moments, modes, normalization terms, and key interpretations. It explains the conjugate relationships beta–Bernoulli/binomial and Dirichlet–multinomial, endpoint or boundary behavior, special cases, the binomial’s Gaussian approximation, and the Dirichlet’s digamma-based expected logarithms and entropy.

nodes.title: Gamma
nodes.summary: The text introduces the Gamma and Gaussian probability distributions, giving their parameter constraints, densities, moments, modes, expected log value where applicable, and entropies. It explains Gamma–Gaussian conjugacy, identifies the exponential distribution as the Gamma special case with a = 1, defines precision and standard deviation, and describes the conjugate priors for Gaussian parameters. It concludes by beginning the multivariate Gaussian description in terms of a mean vector and symmetric covariance matrix.

nodes.title: Gaussian
nodes.summary: The text presents the Gamma, univariate and multivariate Gaussian, Gaussian-gamma, Gaussian-Wishart, and multinomial probability distributions. It gives their parameter constraints, densities, moments, modes, entropies, precision relationships, conjugate-prior roles, and key Gaussian properties, including affine transformations, marginalization, conditioning, and block-partition formulas. It concludes with the one-hot multinomial distribution and its moments, covariances, and entropy.

nodes.title: Gaussian-Gamma
nodes.summary: The text presents a Gaussian marginal distribution, defines the Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart conjugate priors for unknown Gaussian means and precisions, notes their scalar equivalence, and introduces the K-category multinomial distribution along with its probability form, moments, covariances, and entropy.

nodes.title: Gaussian-Wishart
nodes.summary: The text presents a Gaussian marginal, the Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart conjugate priors for unknown Gaussian parameters, their scalar relationship, and the definition, moments, covariance, and entropy of a one-hot multinomial distribution.

nodes.title: Multinomial
nodes.summary: The text presents Gaussian marginal distributions and conjugate priors for Gaussian parameters, including the Gaussian-Gamma and Gaussian-Wishart distributions. It then develops categorical and multinomial distributions, giving their constraints, probabilities, entropy, moments, covariance structure, combinatorial coefficient, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. It also explains terminology relating normal and Gaussian distributions and introduces the Student’s t-distribution as a Gaussian precision mixture obtained by marginalizing a Gamma-distributed precision.

nodes.title: Normal
nodes.summary: The text presents the multinomial distribution, its probability formula, parameter constraints, combinatorial coefficient, means, variances, covariances, and Dirichlet conjugate prior. It then clarifies terminology equating the normal distribution with the Gaussian and describes related naming conventions, before introducing the historical origin and Gaussian-mixture derivation of the univariate Student’s t-distribution.

nodes.title: Student’s t
nodes.summary: The text covers the multinomial distribution, including its probability formula, parameter constraints, moments, covariances, combinatorial coefficient, and Dirichlet conjugate prior; clarifies the terminology linking normal and Gaussian distributions; explains the origin, univariate and multivariate forms, moments, special cases, limiting Gaussian behavior, and robustness of Student’s t-distribution; and presents the uniform distribution with its density, moments, entropy, and interval-transformation property.

nodes.title: Uniform
nodes.summary: The text presents the univariate and multivariate Student’s t-distributions, including their densities, moments, modes, degrees-of-freedom interpretation, Cauchy special case, Mahalanobis-distance formulation, Gaussian limiting case, and robustness to outliers. It then defines the continuous uniform distribution on [a,b], giving its density, mean, variance, entropy, and affine transformation from a standard uniform variable.

nodes.title: Von Mises
nodes.summary: The text defines the von Mises circular distribution, its periodicity, interpretation, parameters, and Gaussian approximation for high concentration. It then presents the Wishart distribution as the conjugate prior for a multivariate Gaussian precision matrix, giving its density and normalization, mean, expected log determinant, entropy, parameter restrictions, and its reduction to a one-dimensional gamma distribution.

nodes.title: Wishart
nodes.summary: The text presents the von Mises circular distribution, including its density, periodicity, interpretation of its location and concentration parameters, origin-dependence of ordinary expectations, and Gaussian approximation for high concentration. It then describes the Wishart distribution as a conjugate prior for multivariate Gaussian precision matrices, providing its density, normalization constant, mean, expected log determinant, entropy, parameter constraints, matrix assumptions, and its reduction to a one-dimensional gamma distribution.

structure.summary: Appendix B surveys common probability distributions and their statistics, parameterizations, densities or mass functions, moments, modes, entropies, normalization terms, approximations, special cases, and interpretations. It covers Bernoulli, beta, binomial, Dirichlet, Gamma, univariate and multivariate Gaussian, Gaussian-Gamma, Gaussian-Wishart, categorical and multinomial, Student's t, uniform, von Mises, and Wishart distributions. The appendix emphasizes conjugate relationships, including beta-Bernoulli/binomial, Dirichlet-multinomial, Gamma-Gaussian, and Wishart-Gaussian models; Gaussian transformations, marginalization, and conditioning; Gaussian-mixture derivation and robustness of Student's t; and relevant boundary behavior, limiting cases, circular properties, and matrix formulations.

structure.title: Appendix C. Properties of Matrices

nodes.title: Basic Matrix Identities
nodes.summary: The text introduces an appendix of standard matrix and determinant properties for readers familiar with linear algebra. It defines matrix notation, identity, transpose, inverse, linear independence, rank, trace, and determinant, and presents transpose and inverse rules, computationally useful inverse identities including a special case and the Woodbury identity, along with trace commutation and cyclic properties. It also notes assumptions about invertibility and dimensions, indicates proof methods, and cites standard references.

nodes.title: Traces and Determinants
nodes.summary: The text develops matrix properties and identities, including inverse rearrangements, the special inverse relation, and the Woodbury identity with dimensionality-based computational advantages. It defines linear independence and matrix rank, then covers trace properties and cyclicity, determinant definitions and key product, inverse, rectangular, and rank-one identities. It concludes by defining vector and matrix derivatives componentwise and stating the derivative of x^Ta with respect to x.

nodes.title: Matrix Derivatives
nodes.summary: The text presents fundamental determinant identities, including permutation-based and 2×2 definitions, product and inverse rules, Sylvester’s determinant theorem, and the rank-one determinant lemma. It then introduces vector and matrix derivatives and lists product, inverse, log-determinant, and trace differentiation rules, concluding with the eigenvector equation for a square matrix.

nodes.title: Eigenvector Equation
nodes.summary: The text presents key matrix-calculus derivative rules for products, inverses, determinants, and traces, then develops eigenvalues and eigenvectors of square matrices, with emphasis on real symmetric matrices. It explains characteristic equations, real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenbases, orthogonal transformations, diagonalization, spectral expansions, determinant and trace formulas, and inverse representations. It concludes by defining positive-definite and positive-semidefinite matrices through quadratic forms and eigenvalue signs, emphasizing that positive definiteness does not require all matrix entries to be positive.

structure.summary: This appendix reviews foundational matrix algebra, traces, determinants, matrix calculus, and eigenvalue theory. It defines core matrix concepts and records transpose, inverse, Woodbury, trace, determinant, rectangular, and rank-one identities; introduces componentwise vector and matrix derivatives with product, inverse, determinant, log-determinant, and trace rules; and develops eigenvectors and spectral decompositions of square, especially real symmetric, matrices. It concludes with determinant, trace, inverse, and definiteness characterizations based on eigenvalues and quadratic forms, while noting dimensionality, invertibility, computational considerations, and standard references.

structure.title: Appendix D. Calculus of Variations
structure.summary: The appendix introduces functionals and the calculus of variations, illustrating them with curve length and entropy. It develops the functional derivative by perturbing a function with an arbitrary variation, establishes that stationarity requires the derivative to vanish, and derives the Euler–Lagrange equation for integral functionals involving a function and its derivative. An example yields a second-order differential equation, while derivative-free integrands reduce to a pointwise condition. The text also discusses boundary conditions, normalization constraints handled by Lagrange multipliers, multidimensional extensions, and a reference for further reading.

structure.title: Appendix E. Lagrange Multipliers
structure.summary: The appendix explains Lagrange multipliers for finding stationary points of functions subject to equality and inequality constraints. It motivates the method geometrically: gradients of constraint functions are normal to constraint surfaces, and at a constrained optimum the objective gradient is parallel or antiparallel to them. For an equality constraint, the Lagrangian L = f + λg is made stationary with respect to both the variables and multiplier, producing the constraint and D + 1 simultaneous equations; a worked quadratic example yields (1/2, 1/2) and λ = 1. For inequality constraints, the constraint can be inactive or active, leading to the sign condition on the multiplier and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions of feasibility, nonnegative multipliers, and complementary slackness. The sign-adjusted formulation for minimization, the extension to multiple equality and inequality constraints, and the applicability to constrained functional derivatives are also stated.
